articles.title: The Azure–AWS Rosetta: every concept and service pair with fidelity
articles.scope: Master table of concept and service pairs grouped by capability, generated from one schema-validated dataset in which fidelity must be exact, close, partial or none and every row carries direction, status (GA, preview, retiring, closed to new customers, with dates) and a last-verified date. Explains the rubric with calibrated exact rows (Kubernetes API, PostgreSQL and MySQL engines, Terraform language, OCI images), asymmetric rows such as Key Vault vs KMS, and exam-vs-current-name callouts. Each row links to its deep article, both provider pages and the reference/ limits tables, so the reader can translate any service name and know how far to trust the translation.

articles.title: Thinking in AWS when you think in Azure (and back): the structural shifts
articles.scope: Teaches the structural differences that change designs: tenant vs account boundary, resource groups vs no container, resource IDs vs ARNs and partitions, one Azure Policy engine vs split AWS controls, region-wide vs AZ-scoped subnets, implicit system routes vs explicit route tables, role assignments vs policy documents and resource policies, free inter-zone traffic on Azure vs billed cross-AZ traffic on AWS, and where each provider draws the shared responsibility line. Each shift comes with a side-by-side example. Afterwards the reader can predict where an Azure-trained design will break on AWS and vice versa.

articles.title: False friends: same name, different behaviour on Azure and AWS
articles.scope: A filtered view of the Rosetta dataset (rows flagged false friend): the two Gateway Load Balancers (Azure's is chained to public frontends and can't be a UDR next hop), NAT gateways (SKUs vs availability modes), Firewall Managers, NSGs vs security groups, resource groups vs AWS Resource Groups, backup vaults, zone numbering, savings plans, Event Grid vs EventBridge, DDoS Protection vs Shield, and 'global' load balancing. Each entry states the assumption, the real behaviour and the exam trap. Use it as a pre-exam and pre-design checklist.

articles.title: Azure Well-Architected and CAF vs AWS Well-Architected and AWS CAF
articles.scope: Maps Azure Well-Architected's five pillars to AWS Well-Architected's six (Sustainability), compares review tooling (Azure Well-Architected Review and Advisor vs the AWS Well-Architected Tool, lenses and Trusted Advisor) and gives mapping tables between Microsoft CAF methodologies and AWS CAF perspectives. The frameworks themselves are taught in architecture/well-architected and the migration-strategy taxonomy in architecture/migration. Afterwards the reader can run a review on either cloud and translate findings between vocabularies.

articles.title: Running one system across Azure and AWS: identity, interconnect, security, observability and egress
articles.scope: Reference pattern for a workload or estate spanning both clouds: workload identity federation in both directions (Entra tokens to AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity; STS GetWebIdentityToken to an Entra federated credential), private interconnect options, unified posture and SIEM (Defender for Cloud's AWS connector, Sentinel's AWS connectors, Arc for EC2), OpenTelemetry-based observability, data replication and the egress bill. Uses the reader's .NET and Angular stack as the running example. Afterwards the reader can design, secure and cost a two-cloud deployment and record the trade-offs in an ADR.

articles.title: Regions, availability zones, partitions and sovereign clouds: Azure vs AWS
articles.scope: Compares paired and nonpaired Azure regions with independent AWS Regions, logical-to-physical zone mapping on both (AZ IDs vs List Locations and Check Zone Peers), zone counts, zonal vs zone-redundant vs regional services, Azure's zone-by-zone update rollout, global services, and sovereign clouds and partitions (Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet vs aws-us-gov and aws-cn). Includes the inter-zone data-transfer difference and a placement decision table. Afterwards the reader can choose regions and zone strategies and explain residency and blast-radius consequences on both clouds.

articles.title: Hybrid and edge platforms: Azure Arc, Azure Local, AKS Arc and Extended Zones vs Outposts, EKS Anywhere, EKS Hybrid Nodes, ECS Anywhere, Local Zones and Wavelength
articles.scope: Compares Azure Arc (servers, Kubernetes, data services), Azure Local, AKS enabled by Azure Arc and Extended Zones with Outposts, EKS Anywhere, EKS Hybrid Nodes, ECS Anywhere, Systems Manager hybrid nodes, Local Zones and Wavelength. Contrasts the ownership model (customer hardware managed from Azure vs AWS-owned racks) and how policy, identity and monitoring extend to each. Afterwards the reader can pick a hybrid or edge platform and govern it from either cloud.

articles.title: Identity model: Microsoft Entra tenant vs AWS account, Organization and IAM
articles.scope: Contrasts the Entra tenant (a directory that owns many subscriptions) with the AWS account and the Organization with its single IAM Identity Center instance; principal types (users, groups, service principals vs IAM users, groups, roles, STS sessions); Global Administrator vs root user and centralized root access; and resource IDs vs ARNs and partitions. Includes C# and Python credential-chain samples (DefaultAzureCredential vs the AWS SDK default chain). Afterwards the reader can design break-glass, admin and directory topology on both clouds.

articles.title: Authorization: Azure RBAC role assignments vs AWS IAM policy evaluation
articles.scope: Explains scoped role assignments with inheritance, Actions and DataActions, and deny assignments (platform-created in GA, customer-managed in private preview) against identity policies, resource-based policies, permissions boundaries, session policies, SCPs and RCPs with the full AWS evaluation logic. Covers where Azure keeps data-plane permissions on resources (ADLS ACLs, SAS rules, legacy Key Vault access policies), ABAC on both, cross-account vs cross-subscription access, and effective-access tools (Check access vs policy simulator and Access Analyzer). Afterwards the reader can write least-privilege grants on either cloud and debug an access-denied.

articles.title: Workload identity: managed identities and federation vs IAM roles, Pod Identity and OIDC
articles.scope: Compares system- and user-assigned managed identities with instance profiles and execution or task roles, service principals with secrets vs IAM users with access keys, Entra Workload ID with EKS Pod Identity and IRSA, and federated identity credentials with IAM OIDC providers for GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines. Covers cross-cloud federation in both directions, including IAM outbound identity federation (STS GetWebIdentityToken). Shows C# and Python token acquisition plus Bicep, CloudFormation and Terraform wiring, linking to security/workload-identity rather than repeating it.

articles.title: Human identities: Entra ID vs IAM Identity Center (workforce) and External ID vs Cognito (customers)
articles.scope: Workforce half: Entra ID SSO, Conditional Access, ID Protection, Microsoft-enforced MFA, SSPR and B2B guests vs IAM Identity Center permission sets, IAM condition keys and cross-account roles, with the recommended pattern of Entra ID as the external IdP for Identity Center via SAML and SCIM. Customer half: Microsoft Entra External ID (and legacy Azure AD B2C, closed to new customers) vs Cognito user pools and identity pools. Afterwards the reader can design SSO for engineers across both clouds and pick a CIAM service for an app.

articles.title: Directory services and hybrid identity: Entra Connect, Cloud Sync and Entra Domain Services vs AWS Managed Microsoft AD, AD Connector, Simple AD and Identity Center AD sync
articles.scope: Compares Entra Connect Sync and Cloud Sync (password hash sync, pass-through authentication) with Identity Center sync through AD Connector, AWS Managed Microsoft AD or SCIM, and Entra Domain Services and AD DS on VMs with AWS Managed Microsoft AD, AD Connector and Simple AD, including forest trusts. Afterwards the reader can connect an on-premises Active Directory to either cloud and choose a managed domain for lift-and-shift Windows workloads.

articles.title: Privileged access and identity governance: PIM, access reviews, entitlement management and CIEM vs IAM Identity Center, IAM Access Analyzer and partner just-in-time access
articles.scope: Contrasts PIM for Entra roles, Azure roles and groups, access reviews, entitlement management and Defender CSPM permissions management (CIEM) with IAM Identity Center permission sets, IAM Access Analyzer unused, external and internal access findings, and partner or TEAM-based temporary elevated access, since AWS has no first-party just-in-time access. Covers emergency-access accounts and least-privilege audits on both. Afterwards the reader can design privileged access and recertification for a two-cloud estate.

articles.title: Application authorization: Entra app registrations, app roles and scopes vs Cognito resource servers, API Gateway and ALB authorizers, and Amazon Verified Permissions
articles.scope: Compares Entra app registrations, enterprise apps, app roles, scopes and consent with Cognito resource servers and scopes, API Gateway JWT and Lambda authorizers, ALB authentication, and Amazon Verified Permissions (Cedar), which has no Azure counterpart. Shows the same ASP.NET Core and Python API protected on both, linking to security/iam for OAuth and OIDC and to security/capability-based-authz. Afterwards the reader can secure APIs and SPAs with either provider's identity stack.

articles.title: Resource hierarchy: management groups, subscriptions and resource groups vs Organizations, OUs and accounts
articles.scope: Maps tenant root group, management groups, subscriptions and resource groups to organization root, OUs and accounts, including nesting limits, the missing resource-group concept on AWS, blast radius, quotas, tagging strategy (tag inheritance vs tag policies and cost allocation tags) and billing linkage. Gives reference hierarchies for the same enterprise on both clouds. Afterwards the reader can propose an account or subscription structure and justify it.

articles.title: Guardrails: Azure Policy vs SCPs, RCPs, declarative policies, AWS Config and CloudFormation Hooks
articles.scope: Contrasts Azure Policy's single engine (deny, denyAction, audit, modify, deployIfNotExists, exemptions, initiatives) with AWS's split into preventive (SCPs, RCPs, declarative policies), proactive (CloudFormation Hooks), detective (Config rules, conformance packs) and remediation (Systems Manager Automation) controls, noting that RCPs have no Azure counterpart. Also covers resource locks vs deletion protection, inheritance semantics (additive vs intersection), and Resource Graph vs Config queries and Resource Explorer. Afterwards the reader can implement the same control set on both clouds.

articles.title: Landing zones: Azure landing zones vs AWS Control Tower and Landing Zone Accelerator
articles.scope: Compares the ALZ conceptual architecture, platform vs application landing zones, the ALZ Bicep and Terraform accelerator with Azure Verified Modules and subscription vending with Control Tower (landing zone 4.0, controls-dedicated option, Account Factory and AFT) and the Landing Zone Accelerator on AWS. Covers the Azure Blueprints retirement (2027-01-31) and the path to deployment stacks and template specs. Afterwards the reader can stand up or assess a landing zone on either cloud and map controls between them.

articles.title: Resource sharing and delegation: AWS RAM, VPC sharing and delegated administrators vs Azure cross-subscription RBAC, Lighthouse and shared hub networks
articles.scope: Explains AWS RAM shares, VPC sharing, delegated administrator accounts and cross-account roles against Azure's cross-subscription role assignments in one tenant, Azure Lighthouse for cross-tenant delegation, Compute Gallery sharing and shared hub networks. Shows why Azure has no shared-subnet model (a NIC must be in its VNet's subscription) and how that changes network topology. Afterwards the reader can design central networking and security-tooling administration on both clouds.

articles.title: Azure VNet vs Amazon VPC: address space, subnets, routing and egress
articles.scope: Covers region-wide vs AZ-scoped subnets, implicit system routes and UDRs vs explicit route tables and internet gateways, default outbound access and private-by-default subnets vs the default VPC, NAT Gateway Standard and StandardV2 vs zonal and regional AWS NAT gateways, public IPs and prefixes vs Elastic IPs and IPAM pools, subnet delegation and IPv6. Includes Bicep, CloudFormation and Terraform for the same three-tier network. Afterwards the reader can build equivalent networks and predict egress behaviour.

articles.title: NSGs and ASGs vs security groups and network ACLs
articles.scope: Contrasts stateful NSGs with prioritised allow and deny rules on subnets or NICs against stateful allow-only security groups on ENIs and stateless network ACLs, ASGs vs security-group references, service tags vs managed prefix lists, and Virtual Network Manager security admin rules vs Firewall Manager security-group policies. Shows how to evaluate effective rules on each; flow logs are in the network-monitoring article. Afterwards the reader can segment workloads and troubleshoot blocked traffic on both clouds.

articles.title: Private Endpoint and service endpoints vs AWS PrivateLink and gateway endpoints
articles.scope: Explains per-resource private endpoints vs per-service interface endpoints, service endpoints and policies vs gateway endpoints, Private Link service vs endpoint services, private DNS integration (privatelink zones vs endpoint-managed private DNS), and Network Security Perimeter vs AWS data-perimeter policies. Includes hybrid DNS resolution for private PaaS. Afterwards the reader can design private-only PaaS access and avoid the classic DNS failures.

articles.title: Hub-and-spoke and transit: VNet peering, Virtual WAN, Virtual Network Manager and Route Server vs VPC peering, Transit Gateway, Cloud WAN and VPC Route Server
articles.scope: Covers non-transitive peering on both clouds (Azure can transit through a hub NVA with UDRs; AWS drops such traffic), gateway transit, customer-managed hubs and Virtual Network Manager connectivity vs Virtual WAN hubs and routing intent, Transit Gateway route tables and appliance mode, Cloud WAN segments, Azure Route Server vs VPC Route Server, and the two Gateway Load Balancers' different insertion models. Includes cost-of-transit comparisons. Afterwards the reader can design multi-VNet and multi-VPC topologies with inspection on either cloud.

articles.title: Hybrid and cross-cloud connectivity: ExpressRoute and VPN Gateway vs Direct Connect, Site-to-Site VPN and Client VPN
articles.scope: Compares ExpressRoute circuits, private and Microsoft peering, gateways, Global Reach, FastPath, ExpressRoute Direct and encryption with Direct Connect connections, private, public and transit virtual interfaces, Direct Connect gateways, SiteLink and MACsec, plus site-to-site and point-to-site VPN vs Site-to-Site VPN and Client VPN and their resiliency models. Ends with Azure-to-AWS links: VPN between gateways, colocation or partner fabrics, and AWS Interconnect - multicloud, whose Azure integration is in preview. Afterwards the reader can design resilient hybrid and cross-cloud links.

articles.title: Azure DNS, Private Resolver and Traffic Manager vs Amazon Route 53
articles.scope: Covers public and private zones, alias records, auto-registration, DNS Private Resolver forwarding rulesets vs Route 53 Resolver endpoints and rules shared through RAM, DNS resolver policy vs Resolver DNS Firewall, and Traffic Manager profiles vs Route 53 routing policies and health checks. Shows hybrid DNS for both clouds with on-premises. Afterwards the reader can design name resolution and DNS-based failover on each cloud.

articles.title: Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway vs NLB, ALB and Gateway Load Balancer
articles.scope: Compares L4 Azure Load Balancer (HA ports, outbound rules) with NLB, L7 Application Gateway v2 and WAF_v2 with ALB, Application Gateway for Containers with the AWS Load Balancer Controller, and the two Gateway Load Balancers. Covers health probes, TLS, autoscaling and pricing units, and links to the global tier in the edge article. Afterwards the reader can pick and configure the right regional load balancer on either cloud.

articles.title: Global edge: Azure Front Door and the global load balancer vs CloudFront and Global Accelerator
articles.scope: Contrasts Front Door Standard/Premium (CDN, global L7 routing, WAF, Private Link origins, rules engine) with CloudFront (caching, VPC origins, CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge, which Azure can't match), and Global Accelerator with the Azure Load Balancer global tier (formerly cross-region load balancer; the AZ-700 outline still says cross-region). Flags the Front Door (classic) retirement on 2027-03-31 and gives a global-routing decision table with Traffic Manager and Route 53. Afterwards the reader can design global entry points with private origins on both clouds.

articles.title: Network protection: Azure Firewall, WAF and DDoS Protection vs AWS Network Firewall, AWS WAF and Shield
articles.scope: Compares Azure Firewall tiers (IDPS, TLS inspection) and secured virtual hubs with AWS Network Firewall, both Firewall Managers, Azure WAF on Front Door and Application Gateway with AWS WAF web ACLs, and DDoS Protection with Shield Standard and Advanced. Shows centralised-inspection designs on both and links to security/network-security for vendor-neutral concepts. Afterwards the reader can place and configure network protection consistently across both clouds.

articles.title: Network monitoring and troubleshooting: Network Watcher, Connection monitor, VNet flow logs, Traffic Analytics and VNet TAP vs Reachability Analyzer, Network Access Analyzer, VPC Flow Logs, Traffic Mirroring and CloudWatch network monitors
articles.scope: Compares Network Watcher (IP flow verify, next hop, effective security rules, connection troubleshoot), Connection monitor, VNet flow logs with Traffic Analytics and virtual network TAP (preview) with VPC Reachability Analyzer, Network Access Analyzer, VPC Flow Logs, Traffic Mirroring, and CloudWatch Network Synthetic Monitor and Network Flow Monitor. Separates configuration analysis from active probing on each. Afterwards the reader can troubleshoot connectivity and investigate flows on either cloud.

articles.title: Zero-trust access to private apps: Microsoft Entra Private Access, Internet Access and application proxy vs AWS Verified Access and Client VPN
articles.scope: Compares Global Secure Access (Microsoft Entra Private Access and Internet Access) and Entra application proxy with AWS Verified Access and Client VPN for reaching private apps without broad network access. Covers identity and device signals, connectors vs Verified Access endpoints and policies, and the lack of an AWS secure web gateway. Afterwards the reader can replace VPN-based access to private apps on either cloud.

articles.title: Azure VMs, Virtual Machine Scale Sets and Compute Fleet vs EC2, Auto Scaling and EC2 Fleet
articles.scope: Covers sizes vs instance types, images (Compute Gallery and VM Image Builder vs AMIs and EC2 Image Builder), availability sets, proximity placement groups and zones vs placement groups, Spot, Dedicated Hosts, hibernation, scale sets and Compute Fleet vs Auto Scaling groups and EC2 Fleet, Trusted Launch vs NitroTPM, disk encryption, and moving VMs. Closes with specialised compute: Batch, CycleCloud vs ParallelCluster, and Azure VMware Solution vs VMware Cloud on AWS and Amazon EVS. Afterwards the reader can design equivalent VM estates.

articles.title: Fleet and configuration management: Azure Arc, Update Manager, Machine Configuration, Automation and Run Command vs AWS Systems Manager
articles.scope: Compares Azure Arc-enabled servers, Update Manager, Machine Configuration, Automation runbooks and State Configuration, Run Command, Change Tracking and Inventory, and Bastion and JIT access with Systems Manager hybrid activations, Patch Manager, State Manager, Automation, Run Command, Inventory and Session Manager. Notes that Systems Manager Incident Manager is closed to new customers. Afterwards the reader can patch, configure and operate the same mixed fleet from either cloud.

articles.title: Azure App Service and Static Web Apps vs Elastic Beanstalk, ECS Express Mode and Amplify Hosting
articles.scope: Compares App Service plans, deployment slots, Easy Auth, VNet integration, certificates, custom domains and backups with Elastic Beanstalk environments and URL swaps, ECS Express Mode (the recommended path now that App Runner is closed to new customers) and Amplify Hosting vs Static Web Apps. Focuses on hosting a .NET API plus Angular front end on each. Afterwards the reader can map an App Service estate to AWS and back.

articles.title: End-user computing: Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365 vs Amazon WorkSpaces and Amazon WorkSpaces Applications
articles.scope: Compares Azure Virtual Desktop host pools, multi-session Windows and RemoteApp, and Windows 365 Cloud PCs with Amazon WorkSpaces Personal and Pools and Amazon WorkSpaces Applications (formerly Amazon AppStream 2.0). Covers identity, networking, image management and pricing models. Afterwards the reader can choose a virtual desktop or app-streaming service on either cloud.

articles.title: AKS vs EKS: control plane, nodes, networking, identity and add-ons
articles.scope: Covers pricing tiers and support windows (AKS LTS vs EKS extended support), AKS Automatic vs EKS Auto Mode, node autoprovisioning vs Karpenter, node pools vs node groups, CNIs (Azure CNI Overlay and Cilium vs VPC CNI), Application Gateway for Containers vs the Load Balancer Controller, Workload ID vs Pod Identity, the Istio add-on vs life after App Mesh, Fleet Manager, and Defender for Containers vs GuardDuty and Inspector. Kubernetes core concepts stay in devops/kubernetes. Afterwards the reader can run the same workload on either cluster with equivalent security.

articles.title: Azure Container Apps, ACI and Container Registry vs Amazon ECS on Fargate, ECS Express Mode, App Runner and ECR
articles.scope: Contrasts Container Apps (KEDA scaling, revisions, Dapr, jobs, scale-to-zero, serverless GPUs) with ECS services on Fargate, ECS Express Mode and Service Connect, App Runner's closed-to-new-customers status, and ACI container groups vs Fargate tasks. Also covers registries: ACR tiers, artifact cache, geo-replication and ACR Tasks vs ECR pull-through cache, replication and CodeBuild. Afterwards the reader can choose a serverless container platform and registry on each cloud and port between them.

articles.title: Azure Functions vs AWS Lambda
articles.scope: Compares hosting plans (Flex Consumption, Premium, Dedicated, Container Apps, and legacy Linux Consumption retiring 2028-09-30) with Lambda on-demand, provisioned concurrency, SnapStart and Managed Instances; triggers and bindings vs event source mappings; timeouts, memory and cold starts, VNet access and the .NET isolated worker vs the Lambda .NET runtime. Includes the same function in C# and Python on both. Afterwards the reader can port functions and pick the right plan.

articles.title: Logic Apps and Durable Functions vs AWS Step Functions and Lambda durable functions
articles.scope: Contrasts connector-centric Logic Apps (Consumption, Standard) and code-first Durable Functions (including Durable Task Scheduler) with Step Functions Standard and Express workflows and Lambda durable functions, which now have SDKs for C#, Python, Java, Go, JavaScript and TypeScript and run for up to a year. Covers human-approval patterns, agentic orchestration, error handling, long waits and cost models. Afterwards the reader can choose an orchestration style and translate workflows between clouds.

articles.title: Azure API Management vs Amazon API Gateway, including real-time and AI gateways
articles.scope: Compares APIM tiers, policies, products, workspaces, developer portal, self-hosted gateway and AI gateway with API Gateway REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs, usage plans and throttling, authorizers and mapping templates, and with AgentCore Gateway for MCP tools. Also covers managed real-time options (SignalR Service and Web PubSub vs API Gateway WebSocket APIs and AppSync Events), linking to messaging/signalr-websockets. Afterwards the reader can design a governed API layer on both clouds.

articles.title: SaaS integration and notifications: Logic Apps connectors, Data Factory, API Management GraphQL, Communication Services and Notification Hubs vs AppFlow, EventBridge API destinations, AppSync, SES and End User Messaging
articles.scope: Compares Logic Apps connectors and HTTP actions, Data Factory, API Management GraphQL and Data API builder, Communication Services Email and Notification Hubs with Amazon AppFlow, EventBridge API destinations, AWS AppSync, Amazon SES, SNS mobile push and AWS End User Messaging. Afterwards the reader can integrate SaaS systems, GraphQL APIs and notifications on either cloud.

articles.title: Azure Service Bus and Queue Storage vs Amazon SQS, SNS and Amazon MQ
articles.scope: Maps queues, topics and subscriptions, sessions, duplicate detection, scheduled delivery, transactions and dead-lettering to SQS standard and FIFO, SNS fan-out, delay queues and redrive, plus Queue Storage vs SQS and Amazon MQ for protocol compatibility. Includes C# and Python producer and consumer samples on both; size and throughput limits live in reference/. Links to messaging/delivery-semantics and messaging/outbox-pattern.

articles.title: Azure Event Grid vs Amazon EventBridge
articles.scope: Compares system and custom topics, namespaces with pull delivery and the MQTT broker, filters and retries with EventBridge default and custom buses, rules and patterns, archive and replay, schema registry, Pipes, Scheduler and cross-account event buses. Shows the same event-driven flow, including automated remediation, on both. Afterwards the reader can design event routing and know which features have no counterpart.

articles.title: Azure Event Hubs and Stream Analytics vs Kinesis, MSK, Data Firehose and Managed Flink
articles.scope: Compares partitions and throughput or processing units with shards and on-demand mode, the Event Hubs Kafka endpoint with Amazon MSK, Capture with Data Firehose, Stream Analytics with Managed Service for Apache Flink, Fabric Real-Time Intelligence with composed AWS streaming, and the two schema registries. Links to messaging/redis-streams-vs-kafka. Afterwards the reader can choose and size a streaming backbone on either cloud.

articles.title: IoT and device messaging: IoT Hub, Event Grid MQTT broker, IoT Edge, DPS and Defender for IoT vs AWS IoT Core, Greengrass, IoT Device Management and Device Defender
articles.scope: Compares IoT Hub, Device Provisioning Service, IoT Edge, the Event Grid MQTT broker and Defender for IoT with AWS IoT Core, fleet provisioning, Greengrass, IoT Device Management and Device Defender, with status callouts for discontinued IoT services on both clouds. Afterwards the reader can design device connectivity and fleet management on either cloud.

articles.title: Azure Blob Storage vs Amazon S3
articles.scope: Covers storage accounts vs buckets, redundancy (LRS/ZRS/GRS/GZRS vs S3 classes and replication), tiers including smart tier vs Intelligent-Tiering and the Archive tier's redundancy limits, versioning and soft delete vs delete markers and MFA Delete, immutability vs Object Lock, SAS and stored access policies vs presigned URLs, shared keys, encryption options, network rules vs bucket policies, Block Public Access, Requester Pays and Access Points (no Azure counterpart), ADLS hierarchical namespace and malware scanning. Afterwards the reader can configure equivalent, secure object storage on both clouds.

articles.title: Managed disks, Elastic SAN, Azure Files and NetApp Files vs EBS, EFS and FSx
articles.scope: Compares managed disk types (Premium SSD v2, Ultra, ZRS disks, shared disks) and Elastic SAN with EBS volume types and Multi-Attach, Azure Files SMB and NFS with identity-based access against FSx for Windows File Server and EFS, Azure NetApp Files vs FSx for NetApp ONTAP, Managed Lustre vs FSx for Lustre, and FSx for OpenZFS, which has no Azure counterpart. Afterwards the reader can pick block and file storage for performance and cost on each cloud.

articles.title: Hybrid storage and data transfer: Azure File Sync, Blob SFTP, Storage Mover, Data Box and AzCopy vs Storage Gateway, Transfer Family, DataSync, S3 Transfer Acceleration, Snowball Edge and Data Transfer Terminal
articles.scope: Compares Azure File Sync, Blob SFTP and NFS, Storage Mover, Data Box, AzCopy and Storage Explorer with Storage Gateway (S3 File, Volume and Tape Gateway), Transfer Family, DataSync, S3 Transfer Acceleration, Snowball Edge (closed to new customers) and Data Transfer Terminal. Afterwards the reader can choose online, offline and hybrid transfer paths for a migration or ongoing sync on either cloud.

articles.title: Azure Cosmos DB vs Amazon DynamoDB, and the purpose-built NoSQL map
articles.scope: Deep comparison of RU/s vs capacity units, partitioning, consistency levels vs strong or eventual reads and MREC or MRSC global tables, change feed vs Streams, serverless vs on-demand, and the integrated cache vs DAX. A second part maps Cosmos DB's other APIs, Table Storage and Azure DocumentDB to Amazon DocumentDB, Keyspaces and Neptune, and Azure Data Explorer to Timestream. Includes C# and Python data-access samples; vector search is in the vector-stores article.

articles.title: Azure SQL and Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL vs Amazon RDS and Aurora

terms.definition: A four-level judgement (exact, close, partial, none) of how faithfully a service or concept on one cloud reproduces the behaviour, scope and guarantees of its counterpart on the other, stated for a direction of translation.

A pair of identically or similarly named services on Azure and AWS whose behaviour differs enough that assuming equivalence causes design or exam errors, such as the two Gateway Load Balancers, whose insertion models differ, or the two Firewall Managers, which manage different things.

A curated, machine-readable mapping of concepts and services between clouds that records, for each pair, the closest counterpart, its fidelity rating and direction, its lifecycle status and the key behavioural difference.

A cross-cloud mapping whose fidelity differs by direction, for example Azure Key Vault maps only partially to AWS because it splits into KMS, Secrets Manager and ACM, while AWS KMS maps closely to Key Vault keys.

Two services from the same provider that are commonly mistaken for each other, such as Event Grid and Event Hubs or SQS and SNS, documented on the owning provider pages rather than in the cross-cloud Rosetta.

Automated, policy-compliant creation of a new cloud isolation unit (an Azure subscription or an AWS account) with baseline identity, networking, logging and guardrails applied before workload teams receive it.
terms.equivalent: azure: subscription vending with the ALZ subscription-vending Bicep and Terraform modules; aws: AWS Control Tower Account Factory and Account Factory for Terraform (close)

terms.definition: Private connectivity between two cloud providers' networks: an IPsec VPN between their gateways, dedicated circuits such as ExpressRoute and Direct Connect meeting in a shared colocation or partner fabric, or a provider-managed offering such as AWS Interconnect - multicloud, whose Azure integration is in preview.

An isolated group of AWS Regions with its own IAM instance and ARN prefix (aws, aws-cn, aws-us-gov); IAM credentials and cross-Region features such as S3 Cross-Region Replication don't work across partitions.
terms.equivalent: azure: sovereign and national clouds such as Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet, each with separate Entra and Resource Manager endpoints (close)

terms.definition: AWS's account-independent identifier for a physical Availability Zone (for example use1-az1), unlike the AZ name such as us-east-1a, which AWS maps to physical zones separately for each account.
terms.equivalent: azure: physical zone names returned per subscription by the List Locations (availabilityZoneMappings) and Check Zone Peers APIs (close)

terms.definition: The hierarchical path that uniquely identifies an Azure resource, in the form /subscriptions/{id}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/{namespace}/{type}/{name}, which also serves as the scope string for role and policy assignments.

The effort needed to move a workload from one provider to another without redesigning it, traded off against the productivity of provider-native managed services; a fidelity rating is in effect a portability estimate for one service pair.

A per-GB fee a provider bills when data crosses a zone, region, peering link, NAT gateway, endpoint or the provider's network edge; Azure doesn't charge for transfer between availability zones in a region, while AWS bills most cross-AZ traffic in each direction.

Moving workloads from one public cloud provider to another, for example AWS to Azure with Azure Migrate or Azure to AWS with AWS Application Migration Service, which adds identity remapping, egress cost and service translation to the usual migration work.

A set of preventive guardrails ensuring only trusted identities access trusted resources from expected networks, assembled on AWS from SCPs, RCPs and VPC endpoint policies and approximated on Azure with Network Security Perimeter, private endpoints, disabled shared-key access and Conditional Access.

pairs.difference: Both are CNCF-conformant for the same minor versions, so manifests that use only upstream APIs port unchanged; the managed services around them (AKS vs EKS) are only close.

pairs.a: Community PostgreSQL and MySQL engines on Azure Database flexible server
pairs.b: Community PostgreSQL and MySQL engines on Amazon RDS
pairs.difference: Same open-source engines and wire protocols; supported versions, extension allow-lists and superuser restrictions differ, and the managed services around them are close rather than exact.

pairs.a: pgvector on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server
pairs.b: pgvector on Aurora PostgreSQL or RDS for PostgreSQL
pairs.difference: Same open-source extension and SQL; available extension versions and index types (HNSW, IVFFlat) depend on each service's supported release.

pairs.a: Terraform language (HCL) and core workflow on Azure
pairs.b: Terraform language (HCL) and core workflow on AWS
pairs.difference: Identical language, CLI, plan and apply workflow and state model; only providers, authentication and backends differ.

pairs.a: OCI image format and registry API (Azure Container Registry)
pairs.b: OCI image format and registry API (Amazon ECR)
pairs.difference: Both implement the OCI image, artifact and distribution specifications, so images, Helm charts and signatures push and pull with the same tools; authentication and repository policy differ.

Many Azure regions, mostly older ones, are paired and newer ones are often nonpaired, so GRS and geo-replication targets vary by region; AWS Regions are never paired. Azure also rolls updates out one zone at a time within a region.

Both map logical to physical zones per subscription or account; AWS publishes stable AZ IDs (use1-az1) while Azure returns physical zones through List Locations or Check Zone Peers. Every AWS Region has at least three AZs, some Azure regions have none, and only AWS bills cross-zone traffic.
AWS has no paired-region construct, so every cross-Region replication target is chosen per service; on Azure, GRS and some platform defaults follow the pair where one exists.

Azure often makes zone redundancy a SKU or setting on one resource (ZRS storage, StandardV2 NAT Gateway); AWS more often has you place one resource per AZ (subnets, zonal NAT gateways) unless the service is regional.
Both are isolated US government clouds with separate endpoints; GovCloud is a separate AWS partition (aws-us-gov) that needs separate accounts and ARNs.
Both are operated by local partners with separate accounts, endpoints and identity, and their service catalogs lag the global clouds.

pairs.a: Microsoft Sovereign Cloud offerings in Europe (verify)
pairs.difference: AWS's offering is a separately operated EU-only cloud, while Microsoft layers data-boundary and operational sovereignty controls on Azure regions and partner-operated national clouds; verify availability and the AWS partition name before writing.
Extended Zones need an access request and offer a subset of services (AKS is GA); Local Zones are opt-in extensions of a parent Region with broader EC2, EBS and ELB coverage in many metro areas.

pairs.a: (no current Azure equivalent; verify any carrier-edge offering)
pairs.difference: Wavelength Zones put EC2, EBS and EKS inside carrier 5G networks reached through a carrier gateway; Azure has no generally available carrier-edge zone today.
Azure Local runs on customer-procured validated hardware managed through Azure Arc; Outposts is AWS-owned hardware that AWS installs, monitors and services.

pairs.b: Systems Manager hybrid nodes, EKS Hybrid Nodes and ECS Anywhere
pairs.difference: Arc projects any server or Kubernetes cluster as an Azure resource governed by Azure Policy and RBAC; AWS spreads hybrid management across service-specific agents.

Both run the provider's Kubernetes distribution on customer hardware; AKS Arc runs on Azure Local or Windows Server and is managed from Azure, EKS Anywhere runs on vSphere, bare metal and other targets.

pairs.b: EKS Hybrid Nodes and EKS Connector
pairs.difference: Arc attaches any conformant cluster to Azure for policy, GitOps and monitoring; EKS Hybrid Nodes join on-premises machines to a cloud EKS control plane, and EKS Connector only registers external clusters for viewing.
A tenant is a directory boundary that can own many subscriptions; an AWS account is resource container, billing unit and IAM boundary in one.

pairs.b: AWS Organization with its IAM Identity Center instance
pairs.difference: Both are the top-level boundary an enterprise usually has one of; a tenant is also the directory and IdP for every subscription, while an Organization groups accounts for policy and billing and its single Identity Center instance holds or syncs the workforce identities.

Entra ID is a global directory and IdP for users, apps, SSO and MFA; IAM is a per-account authorization system of principals and JSON policies, not a workforce directory, and its authorization role maps to Azure RBAC instead.

Identity Center provides SSO and permission sets across an organization but usually federates to an external IdP such as Entra ID; it has no Conditional Access, risk scoring, device signals or broad SaaS app gallery.
IAM users are account-local principals with long-term credentials that AWS recommends avoiding; Entra users are tenant-wide identities used across all subscriptions and SaaS apps.
Entra groups can be dynamic, role-assignable and tenant-wide; IAM groups are account-local, can't be nested and can't be a principal in a resource policy.

pairs.a: Entra B2B guest users and cross-tenant access settings
pairs.b: Cross-account role assumption or Identity Center with an external IdP
pairs.difference: B2B lets a partner's identities sign in to your tenant as guests governed by your Conditional Access; AWS lets external principals assume roles your accounts trust, optionally with an external ID.

The root user is an unrestrictable per-account identity created with the account (Organizations can remove member-account root credentials centrally); Global Administrator is a directory role that must elevate access to manage Azure resources.

pairs.a: Microsoft-enforced MFA for Azure management and security defaults
pairs.b: MFA enforcement for root users and IAM Identity Center MFA settings
pairs.difference: Microsoft enforces MFA for portal, CLI, PowerShell and IaC sign-ins to Azure; AWS enforces MFA for root users and lets you require it in Identity Center, while IAM principals rely on conditions such as aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent.

pairs.b: IAM Identity Center identity-store password reset
pairs.difference: SSPR covers cloud and, with writeback, hybrid users with configurable methods; Identity Center's self-service reset applies only to users in its own identity store, not to users federated from an external IdP.

pairs.a: Microsoft Entra Connect Sync or Cloud Sync
pairs.b: IAM Identity Center sync from AD (AD Connector or AWS Managed Microsoft AD) or SCIM
pairs.difference: Entra Connect and Cloud Sync synchronize on-premises users, including password hashes, into the tenant; Identity Center syncs users and groups from AD through Directory Service or receives them over SCIM, with no password hash sync.
Entra Domain Services is a synced managed domain without Domain Admins; Managed Microsoft AD is a real forest you administer as delegated admin that can trust an on-premises forest.
AD Connector proxies authentication to an on-premises AD without caching identities in AWS, and Simple AD is a Samba-based directory; Azure's options are Entra Domain Services or AD DS on VMs.

Both grant full control; Owner also allows role assignment within its scope and can be time-bound through PIM, whereas AdministratorAccess applies per account unless an SCP or permissions boundary caps it.

pairs.b: AWS managed policies for job functions
pairs.difference: Both are provider-maintained permission bundles; Azure built-ins are bound at a chosen scope by an assignment, AWS managed policies are attached to principals and scoped by their Resource element.

A role definition lists Actions, NotActions, DataActions and assignable scopes but has no Resource or Condition elements, because scope lives on the role assignment; an IAM policy carries Effect, Action, Resource and Condition in one document.

pairs.a: Azure role assignment at a scope
pairs.b: Attached IAM policy or Identity Center permission set assignment
pairs.difference: An Azure assignment binds principal, role and scope with inheritance down the hierarchy; AWS scoping lives inside each policy's Resource and Condition elements per account.

An AWS explicit Deny can be written in any policy and always wins; in GA, Azure deny assignments are created only by the platform (deployment stack deny settings, managed applications), and customer-managed deny assignments are in private preview.

pairs.a: Azure RBAC at resource scope and service-specific data-plane permissions
pairs.difference: Azure has no general resource policy document, though some services keep data-plane permissions on the resource (legacy Key Vault access policies, ADLS Gen2 ACLs, Service Bus and Event Hubs SAS rules, stored access policies); none grants another tenant's identity access the way a bucket policy grants another account access.

pairs.b: IAM ABAC with principal, session and resource tags
pairs.difference: Azure ABAC adds conditions to role assignments, mainly for Blob and Queue data actions and constrained delegation; AWS ABAC matches principal or session tags against resource tags across most services.

pairs.a: Azure Check access and effective permissions
pairs.b: IAM policy simulator and Access Analyzer policy validation
pairs.difference: Check access shows a principal's role and deny assignments at a scope; AWS simulates a request against all applicable policy types and validates policies, including checks for public and cross-account access.

pairs.b: Cross-account IAM roles and Organizations delegated administrator
pairs.difference: Lighthouse projects a provider tenant's identities into customer subscriptions with RBAC; AWS cross-account access works by assuming roles each account trusts.

pairs.b: IAM condition keys and Identity Center MFA settings
pairs.difference: Conditional Access evaluates user, device, risk and location at sign-in for every app; AWS evaluates request-time conditions such as source IP or MFA presence per API call, with no device or risk signal.

pairs.b: (no first-party AWS equivalent; partner temporary elevated access or the TEAM open-source solution)
pairs.difference: PIM gives approval-gated, time-bound activation of Entra roles, Azure roles and groups; IAM Identity Center has no built-in just-in-time access and integrates with validated partner solutions instead.

pairs.a: Entra ID Governance access reviews and entitlement management
pairs.difference: Access reviews recertify access on a schedule and entitlement management packages access with approval and expiry; AWS reports unused access in IAM Access Analyzer but has no review or request workflow.

pairs.b: IAM Access Analyzer unused, external and internal access findings
pairs.difference: Both flag excessive or unused permissions; Defender's CIEM spans Azure, AWS and GCP identities in one view, while Access Analyzer covers AWS accounts and organizations and also proves external and internal access paths.
ID Protection scores user and sign-in risk to drive Conditional Access; AWS has no workforce sign-in risk engine (GuardDuty flags anomalous API use instead).

pairs.b: IAM role for compute (instance profile, execution or task role)
pairs.difference: Both deliver auto-rotated short-lived credentials to workloads; a managed identity is an Entra service principal, an IAM role is assumed through STS under a trust policy.

pairs.a: Service principal with client secret or certificate
pairs.difference: Both are long-lived credentials for non-human callers that each provider recommends replacing with managed identities, roles or federation; a service principal is tenant-wide, an IAM user is account-local.

pairs.b: IAM OIDC identity provider with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
pairs.difference: Both exchange an external OIDC token, for example from GitHub Actions, for cloud credentials; Entra binds trust to one identity by issuer and subject, AWS by trust-policy conditions.

pairs.a: Managed identity token presented to AWS (Azure-to-AWS federation)
pairs.b: IAM outbound identity federation with STS GetWebIdentityToken (AWS-to-Azure federation)
pairs.difference: Both let a workload prove its identity to the other cloud with a short-lived signed JWT; AWS must enable outbound federation per account and issues tokens lasting 1 to 60 minutes (default 5), which an Entra federated credential then trusts.
AKS federates Kubernetes service-account tokens to an Entra identity; EKS Pod Identity uses an agent and association API, while IRSA uses the cluster's OIDC issuer.

Both are CIAM services with hosted sign-in and social IdPs; Cognito adds identity pools that trade tokens for AWS credentials, and Azure AD B2C is the legacy service, closed to new customers since May 1, 2025.

Agent ID makes agents first-class directory identities governed by Conditional Access and Entra roles (extended security features need Microsoft Agent 365); AgentCore Identity is a credential broker and token vault that lets agents act for users with any IdP, including Entra ID.

pairs.a: Entra app registration with app roles and scopes
pairs.b: Cognito resource server scopes plus API Gateway or ALB authorizers
pairs.difference: An app registration defines an API's scopes and app roles and Entra issues tokens for it; on AWS, Cognito resource servers define scopes and API Gateway JWT or Cognito authorizers, or ALB authentication, enforce them.
Verified Permissions is a managed Cedar policy store and decision API for fine-grained application authorization; on Azure you combine app roles, groups and your own policy engine.
Both nest and inherit controls (management groups up to six levels below root, OUs up to five); management groups carry Azure Policy and RBAC, OUs carry SCPs, RCPs and other organization policies.
Both are billing and quota boundaries; the AWS account is also the hard security boundary, whereas all subscriptions in a tenant trust the same Entra directory.

pairs.b: (no exact equivalent; AWS Resource Groups or CloudFormation stacks)
pairs.difference: Every Azure resource lives in exactly one resource group that scopes RBAC, policy, locks and deletion; AWS resources sit directly in an account and Region and are grouped only by tags or stacks.

pairs.a: Azure tags (inheritance through Policy and Cost Management)
pairs.b: AWS tags, activated cost allocation tags and tag policies
pairs.difference: Azure tags can be inherited from resource groups or subscriptions through Policy modify effects or Cost Management tag inheritance; AWS tags must be activated for billing, and tag policies standardize keys and values without applying tags.
SCPs filter the IAM permissions of principals and can't inspect resource properties beyond condition keys; Azure Policy evaluates the resource payload itself on every Resource Manager write.
Azure Policy combines preventive, detective and remediation effects in one engine; AWS splits them across SCPs and RCPs, Config rules with Systems Manager remediation, and CloudFormation Hooks.

pairs.a: (no Azure equivalent; nearest are platform deny assignments, Network Security Perimeter and disabling shared-key, SAS and anonymous access)
pairs.difference: An RCP caps what any principal, including one from an external account, can do to resources in member accounts, for a growing list of services that started with S3, STS, KMS, SQS and Secrets Manager.

pairs.a: Azure Policy deny on compute properties
pairs.difference: Declarative policies enforce baseline EC2, VPC and EBS settings, such as blocking public AMI sharing or requiring IMDSv2, at the service level even for new APIs; Azure Policy evaluates each Resource Manager write against resource properties.
Both bundle parameterised rules; initiatives are assigned at management-group scope with inheritance, conformance packs deploy per account or organization-wide.

pairs.b: Termination or deletion protection plus SCP deny
pairs.difference: Azure locks apply to any resource or scope and override RBAC; AWS offers per-service protection flags or organization-level SCP denies.

pairs.b: AWS Config advanced queries and AWS Resource Explorer
pairs.difference: Resource Graph is a KQL-queryable inventory across every subscription you can read; AWS splits search (Resource Explorer) from configuration queries over Config aggregators.

pairs.a: Azure Machine Configuration (formerly: Azure Policy guest configuration)
pairs.difference: Both audit and enforce OS settings on servers, including hybrid ones; Machine Configuration is assigned through Azure Policy, State Manager through associations with SSM documents.

pairs.b: AWS Config plus Systems Manager Inventory
pairs.difference: Change Tracking records software, file, registry and service changes on Azure and Arc machines; AWS splits OS inventory (Systems Manager Inventory) from resource configuration history (Config).

pairs.b: Control Tower Account Factory and Account Factory for Terraform
pairs.difference: Both automate pre-governed environment creation; AFT runs a GitOps pipeline on Control Tower, Azure supplies AVM-based Bicep and Terraform vending modules.
ALZ is a reference architecture you deploy with your own IaC; Control Tower is a managed service that builds and operates the landing zone and its controls.

Both deploy an opinionated, compliance-oriented landing zone from code; LZA is a CDK-based solution on top of Control Tower, the ALZ accelerator bootstraps Bicep or Terraform pipelines built on Azure Verified Modules.

pairs.a: Cross-subscription RBAC on shared resources and Compute Gallery sharing
pairs.difference: RAM shares specific resource types (subnets, transit gateways, Resolver rules, AMIs and more) with accounts or OUs; Azure shares by granting role assignments across subscriptions in one tenant or through service-specific sharing such as Compute Gallery.

pairs.a: (no Azure equivalent; a NIC can only join a VNet in its own subscription)
pairs.difference: VPC sharing lets participant accounts launch resources into subnets owned by a central networking account; Azure reaches central networking with peered spokes or Virtual WAN instead.

pairs.a: Role assignments at management-group scope for a central security or operations team
pairs.difference: A delegated administrator is a member account registered to run an organization-wide service such as GuardDuty or Security Hub; Azure grants a team rights over all subscriptions with role assignments at a management group, with no separate administrator-account object.

pairs.a: Azure Deployment Environments and managed-application service catalogs
pairs.difference: Both offer curated self-service infrastructure templates with guardrails; Service Catalog shares CloudFormation or Terraform products through portfolios, and AWS Proton, the other self-service option, reached end of support on 2026-10-07.
Both expose adjustable per-region limits with increase requests and usage alerts; Service Quotas also offers quota request templates applied to new accounts in an organization.
Both report provider incidents, planned maintenance and per-resource health with alerts; AWS Health also aggregates events organization-wide and feeds EventBridge.
Both recommend cost, security, reliability and performance fixes; the full set of Trusted Advisor checks depends on the AWS Support plan, while Advisor recommendations are free.

pairs.b: AWS Audit Manager and Security Hub CSPM standards
pairs.difference: Defender maps Azure Policy and benchmark controls to frameworks in one dashboard; AWS splits continuous checks (Security Hub CSPM) from evidence collection (Audit Manager).
Compliance Manager scores Microsoft 365 and Azure controls against regulations with improvement actions; Audit Manager collects AWS evidence continuously against frameworks for auditor-ready reports.
Both publish the provider's audit reports on demand; Artifact also lets you accept agreements such as the BAA for an account or organization.
Both are regional private networks, but Azure subnets span every zone in the region while each AWS subnet lives in exactly one AZ.

Azure historically gave VMs an implicit outbound IP, and VNets created with API versions released after March 31, 2026 (and in the portal) default to private subnets; AWS instances never get egress without an internet gateway or NAT path, but each Region's default VPC ships with an internet gateway, public subnets and auto-assigned public IPv4.

Azure subnets work on implicit system routes and need a route table only to override them; every AWS subnet must be associated with a route table, and internet access exists only through an explicit route to an internet gateway.

Both are static public IPv4 resources; Azure public IPs are zonal or zone-redundant resources attached to NICs, load balancers or gateways, Elastic IPs are regional and attach to ENIs or NAT gateways.

pairs.b: IPAM-provisioned contiguous public IPv4 or BYOIP
pairs.difference: A public IP prefix reserves a contiguous Microsoft-owned block in one call; AWS offers contiguous Amazon-owned IPv4 blocks through IPAM or bring-your-own-IP ranges.
NSGs are stateful with prioritised allow and deny rules and attach to subnets or NICs; security groups are stateful, allow-only and attach to network interfaces.
NACLs are stateless, so return traffic needs explicit rules; NSGs stay stateful even when attached at subnet level.

pairs.b: Security group referencing another security group
pairs.difference: Both let rules target workload groups instead of IP ranges; AWS references can span peered VPCs, application security groups work only inside one VNet.

Service tags name Microsoft-maintained IP ranges for many Azure services in NSGs, UDRs and firewalls; AWS-managed prefix lists cover fewer services (for example S3, DynamoDB, CloudFront origin-facing) in security groups and route tables.
Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB and work through route-table entries; service endpoints cover many Azure PaaS services per subnet and keep the service's public IP.
A private endpoint maps a private IP to one resource instance, such as a single storage account; an interface endpoint maps to a whole regional service, narrowed by endpoint policies.
Both expose your own service to consumers in other networks with connection approval; Private Link service fronts a Standard Load Balancer, endpoint services front an NLB or GWLB.

pairs.b: AWS data perimeter (RCPs, VPC endpoint policies, aws:SourceVpce conditions)
pairs.difference: Network Security Perimeter is a managed logical boundary around PaaS resources with access rules and logs; an AWS data perimeter is a pattern you assemble from several policy types.

Both are non-transitive; Azure lets spokes reach each other through a hub NVA or Azure Firewall with UDRs and share gateways through gateway transit, whereas AWS drops peered traffic not addressed to the peer VPC's CIDR.
Both provide transitive hub routing; a Virtual WAN hub is a Microsoft-managed VNet that also hosts gateways and firewalls, a transit gateway is a regional router with attachments and route tables.
Both offer a managed global network; Cloud WAN uses a declarative core-network policy with segments, Virtual WAN uses hubs with routing intent.

pairs.b: AWS Cloud WAN, Firewall Manager security-group policies and VPC IPAM
pairs.difference: Virtual Network Manager centrally defines connectivity (mesh, hub-and-spoke), security admin rules, routing and IP address management across subscriptions; AWS spreads those jobs across Cloud WAN or Transit Gateway, Firewall Manager and VPC IPAM.

Both let NVAs exchange routes with the virtual network over BGP; Azure Route Server injects routes into every subnet's effective routes, VPC Route Server updates the route tables you associate with it.

Azure GWLB is chained to a Standard public load balancer frontend or a VM's Standard public IP and can't be a UDR next hop, so it inspects only traffic to and from public endpoints (VXLAN); AWS GWLB is reached through GWLB endpoints used as route-table targets, so it inspects north-south and east-west traffic, including via Transit Gateway appliance mode (GENEVE).

pairs.b: NAT gateway (AWS, zonal or regional availability mode)
pairs.difference: Neither Azure SKU needs a route: Standard is zonal, StandardV2 is zone-redundant with IPv6, NAT64, flow logs and 100 Gbps. AWS zonal NAT gateways live in public subnets with per-AZ routes, while a regional NAT gateway needs no public subnet and expands across AZs itself, though subnets still route to its ID and it doesn't support private NAT.

pairs.a: (no Azure NAT Gateway equivalent; VPN Gateway NAT rules or an NVA)
pairs.difference: A private NAT gateway translates overlapping private ranges toward other VPCs or on-premises through a transit or virtual private gateway; Azure NAT Gateway only provides internet egress.

pairs.b: EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint or Session Manager
pairs.difference: Bastion is a managed jump host deployed into the VNet for RDP and SSH; Session Manager needs no inbound ports at all, relying on the SSM agent and IAM.

pairs.b: Session Manager or EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint
pairs.difference: JIT opens NSG or firewall ports to approved source IPs for a limited time; AWS's preferred pattern needs no inbound ports at all.

Both use SR-IOV to bypass the host's virtual switch for lower latency and higher throughput; ENA is standard on current Nitro instances, Accelerated Networking is a per-NIC setting on supported sizes.
Azure VPN gateways deploy into a GatewaySubnet and are sized by SKU; AWS VPN connections terminate on a virtual private gateway or transit gateway and always provide two tunnels.

Both give remote users VPN access with certificate, RADIUS or Entra and SAML authentication; Client VPN is a separate endpoint associated with subnets, point-to-site is a configuration of the VPN gateway.
An ExpressRoute circuit is a logical, redundant pair of links via a provider; Direct Connect connections are individual dedicated or hosted ports that you make redundant yourself.

pairs.b: Direct Connect private or transit virtual interface
pairs.difference: Private peering reaches VNets through an ExpressRoute gateway; private VIFs attach to virtual private gateways or Direct Connect gateways, transit VIFs to transit gateways.
Both reach the provider's public service endpoints over the private circuit; Microsoft peering needs route filters to select services, a public VIF receives AWS public prefixes.
Both let on-premises sites exchange traffic across the provider's backbone; Global Reach links ExpressRoute circuits, SiteLink links Direct Connect locations through a Direct Connect gateway.
Both give you dedicated ports at a peering location; ExpressRoute Direct ports come as a redundant pair, each Direct Connect dedicated connection is a single port you make redundant yourself.
Both host authoritative DNS; Route 53 is also a domain registrar and builds routing policies and health checks into DNS itself.

Both point a record, including the zone apex, at a provider resource and track its changes; Azure aliases target public IPs, Traffic Manager, Front Door or other record sets, Route 53 aliases target ELB, CloudFront, S3 websites, API Gateway and more.
Both resolve only inside linked networks; Azure private zones can auto-register VM records, Route 53 private zones don't.

pairs.b: Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints
pairs.difference: Both forward conditionally between cloud and on-premises; Azure uses forwarding rulesets linked to VNets, AWS uses Resolver rules shared through RAM.

pairs.a: Azure DNS resolver policy (formerly: DNS security policy)
pairs.difference: Both filter and log VNet or VPC DNS queries with allow, block or alert domain lists and provider-managed threat lists.

pairs.b: Route 53 routing policies with health checks
pairs.difference: Both steer traffic through DNS; Traffic Manager is a separate service built on profiles, Route 53 builds policies such as latency, geoproximity and failover into records.
Both are L4; Azure Load Balancer is a pass-through distributor with HA ports and outbound rules, NLB gives static IPs per AZ and can terminate TLS.

pairs.a: Azure Load Balancer global tier (formerly: cross-region load balancer)
pairs.difference: Global Accelerator advertises anycast IPs from AWS edge locations to ALB, NLB, EC2 and Elastic IP endpoints with weights, traffic dials, client affinity and custom routing; Azure's global tier advertises its IP from about 22 participating Azure regions, fronts only public regional Standard Load Balancers, routes by geo-proximity and has no outbound rules.
Both are regional L7 proxies; Application Gateway deploys into a dedicated subnet with WAF_v2 built in, ALB spans AZ subnets and adds Lambda targets and native OIDC authentication.

pairs.b: AWS Load Balancer Controller with ALB
pairs.difference: Both turn Kubernetes Gateway API or Ingress resources into managed L7 load balancing; Application Gateway for Containers is a separate Azure resource driven by an in-cluster controller, the AWS controller provisions ALBs and NLBs per Ingress or Service.

Front Door combines CDN, global L7 load balancing, WAF and Private Link origins in one resource; AWS composes CloudFront, WAF, Shield and optionally Global Accelerator. Front Door (classic) retires on 2027-03-31.

pairs.a: (no Azure equivalent for custom code at the edge; the Front Door rules engine is declarative only)
pairs.difference: CloudFront runs your JavaScript (Functions) or Node.js and Python (Lambda@Edge) on requests and responses at the edge; Front Door offers declarative rule sets for headers, redirects, rewrites and caching (check for any edge-compute preview).
Both are managed stateful firewalls with IDPS and TLS inspection (Premium tier on Azure); Network Firewall uses Suricata-compatible rules and per-AZ endpoints.

Azure Firewall Manager manages Azure Firewall policies and secured hubs; AWS Firewall Manager enforces WAF, Shield Advanced, security group, Network Firewall and DNS Firewall policies across an organization.
Azure WAF policies attach to Front Door or Application Gateway with Microsoft-managed rule sets; AWS WAF web ACLs attach to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync and more.
Both add tuned L3/L4 mitigation, telemetry, rapid response and cost protection; basic always-on protection is free on both clouds.
Both record flow metadata; VNet flow logs replace NSG flow logs and feed Traffic Analytics, VPC Flow Logs publish to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose.

pairs.a: Network Watcher (IP flow verify, next hop, effective security rules)
pairs.b: VPC Reachability Analyzer and Network Access Analyzer
pairs.difference: Both analyse configured paths without sending packets; Azure adds synthetic probing in the same service (connection troubleshoot, Connection monitor), while AWS puts probing in CloudWatch Network Synthetic Monitor and exposure analysis in Network Access Analyzer.
Connection monitor probes from Azure VMs, Arc machines and on-premises agents to any endpoint; Network Synthetic Monitor probes from AWS to on-premises destinations over hybrid links.

Traffic Analytics aggregates VNet flow logs in Log Analytics into topology, top-talker and threat views; Network Flow Monitor uses lightweight agents to measure TCP performance and loss between workloads and AWS services.
Both copy packets from NICs or ENIs to a collector for inspection; VNet TAP is in public preview, Traffic Mirroring is GA on Nitro instances with filters.

VPC Lattice is an application-layer service network that connects and authorizes services across VPCs and accounts with IAM auth policies; Azure combines Private Link, API Management or a service mesh for similar results.

pairs.a: Microsoft Entra Private Access and application proxy
pairs.difference: Both give identity- and device-aware access to private apps without a full VPN; Private Access is part of Global Secure Access with a client and connectors, while Verified Access evaluates Cedar policies per request at its endpoints.
Internet Access is a cloud secure web gateway for workforce traffic; AWS has no first-party secure web gateway for user internet traffic.
Families and naming differ (D/E/F series vs M/R/C families); every Azure VM sits in a resource group and attaches to a VNet NIC, while EC2 offers a wider range of instance types on the Nitro system.
Both manage elastic fleets across zones; an Auto Scaling group launches from a launch template, a scale set is itself the VM collection with orchestration modes.

Both provision a mix of sizes and Spot and on-demand capacity in one request with allocation strategies; Compute Fleet can span up to three regions and has a Launch mode (preview) that hands VMs to an external orchestrator.

pairs.b: EC2 Auto Scaling policies and Application Auto Scaling
pairs.difference: Azure Monitor autoscale is one engine for scale sets, App Service and other resources with metric and schedule rules; AWS uses target-tracking, step, scheduled and predictive policies in EC2 Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling.
Both pack instances physically close for low latency; a proximity placement group can also hold scale sets and availability sets.

Availability sets spread VMs across fault and update domains in one datacenter; spread groups put each instance on distinct hardware and partition groups expose partitions to topology-aware apps such as Hadoop.

pairs.b: Amazon Machine Image (AMI) sharing and copying
pairs.difference: Compute Gallery is a versioned, replicated image catalogue shared through RBAC; AMIs are regional objects copied and shared per account or organization.
Both build and distribute hardened images from recipes; VM Image Builder publishes to Compute Gallery, EC2 Image Builder distributes across Regions and accounts.
Both discount spare capacity with eviction; Azure gives about 30 seconds' notice through Scheduled Events, EC2 a two-minute interruption notice.

pairs.b: EC2 instance metadata notices and EventBridge events
pairs.difference: Both warn a workload about maintenance, eviction or termination; Azure exposes them through the metadata endpoint, AWS through instance metadata and EventBridge.
Both provide single-tenant physical servers for licensing or compliance; EC2 adds host resource groups through License Manager.
Both save RAM to the OS disk and stop compute billing; supported sizes, operating systems and maximum memory differ.

pairs.a: Trusted Launch (Secure Boot, vTPM, boot integrity monitoring)
pairs.difference: Both provide measured, signed boot with a virtual TPM; Trusted Launch is the default security type for new Azure VMs and adds boot integrity monitoring through Defender for Cloud.

pairs.b: EC2 AMD SEV-SNP instances and Nitro Enclaves
pairs.difference: Azure confidential VMs encrypt the whole VM's memory with hardware keys and attest through Microsoft Azure Attestation; EC2 offers SEV-SNP on some families plus Nitro Enclaves, isolated environments carved from an instance.

pairs.a: Encryption at host and customer-managed keys for managed disks
pairs.b: EBS encryption by default with KMS
pairs.difference: Azure always encrypts disks at rest and adds encryption at host and disk encryption sets for customer-managed keys; EBS encryption is an account-level default using AWS-managed or customer KMS keys.

pairs.a: Azure Resource Mover and resource move operations
pairs.b: (no move operation on AWS; copy AMIs and snapshots, or use MGN or Elastic Disaster Recovery)
pairs.difference: Azure can move many resources between resource groups, subscriptions or regions; AWS resources can't move between accounts or Regions and are recreated from copies.
Both orchestrate OS patching with schedules and compliance; Update Manager also patches Arc-enabled servers on-premises and in other clouds.
Both run scripts on VMs without SSH or RDP; Systems Manager targets fleets by tags or resource groups with rate controls, Azure Run Command runs per VM or scale set.
Both run PowerShell or Python operational runbooks; Systems Manager Automation also ships AWS-authored runbooks used by Config and Security Hub remediation.

pairs.a: Azure Monitor alerts with action groups and runbooks for incident response
pairs.b: AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager (closed to new customers)
pairs.difference: Incident Manager adds response plans, on-call schedules and engagement but no longer accepts new customers; Azure composes incident response from alerts, action groups, runbooks and ITSM or chat integrations.
Both schedule batch jobs on managed pools; AWS Batch can run on EC2, Spot, Fargate or EKS.
Both deploy and autoscale HPC clusters with schedulers such as Slurm; CycleCloud is an orchestrator VM you run, ParallelCluster is an open-source CLI and API that builds clusters from CloudFormation.
Both run VMware Cloud Foundation on dedicated bare metal; VMware Cloud on AWS is operated by Broadcom, Azure VMware Solution is a Microsoft first-party service.
Both run VMware Cloud Foundation on dedicated bare-metal hosts; EVS deploys VCF into your own VPC on EC2 bare-metal instances.

pairs.b: Amazon WorkSpaces Pools and Amazon WorkSpaces Applications (formerly: Amazon AppStream 2.0)
pairs.difference: Azure Virtual Desktop offers multi-session Windows and RemoteApp on host pools you size; WorkSpaces Pools give non-persistent desktops and WorkSpaces Applications streams individual apps.
Both are per-user persistent cloud PCs billed monthly; Windows 365 is a SaaS managed through Intune, WorkSpaces Personal runs in your AWS account.
Lightsail bundles a VM, storage, IP and transfer allowance at a fixed monthly price; Azure has no bundled VPS offering.
App Service is a PaaS with plans, slots and built-in auth; Elastic Beanstalk orchestrates EC2, Auto Scaling and load balancer resources that stay visible in your account.
Slots are live staging instances on the same plan swapped after warm-up; Beanstalk swaps CNAMEs between two complete environments.
ECS Express Mode deploys a container image with a load balancer, TLS and autoscaling on Fargate in your account; App Service can also run code without a container.
Both host static front ends such as Angular with Git-based CI/CD and preview environments; Static Web Apps links Functions or Container Apps backends, Amplify Hosting adds SSR for several frameworks.
AKS's Free tier has no control-plane charge, with Standard adding an SLA and Premium long-term support; EKS bills per cluster-hour, more during extended support.
Both extend a Kubernetes minor version's support for a fee; AKS LTS needs the Premium tier, EKS extended support applies automatically unless you upgrade.
Both manage nodes with Karpenter-style autoprovisioning and hardened defaults; AKS Automatic also hosts managed system node pools and adds a pod-readiness SLA.
Node autoprovisioning is Microsoft's managed Karpenter; on EKS you run Karpenter yourself unless you use Auto Mode.

pairs.a: Azure CNI Overlay and Azure CNI powered by Cilium
pairs.difference: Overlay assigns pod IPs from a private range separate from the VNet; the VPC CNI gives each pod a VPC IP by default, with prefix delegation and custom networking to ease IP exhaustion.

pairs.a: Istio-based service mesh add-on for AKS
pairs.b: (AWS App Mesh support ended 2026-09-30; ECS Service Connect, VPC Lattice or self-managed Istio)
pairs.difference: AKS offers a supported Istio add-on; AWS has no managed mesh since App Mesh ended, pointing ECS users to Service Connect and EKS users to VPC Lattice or self-managed meshes.
Fleet Manager orchestrates upgrades, workload placement and multi-cluster networking across AKS clusters; EKS relies on GitOps tools or partner products for that.

pairs.b: GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring plus Inspector ECR scanning
pairs.difference: Defender for Containers bundles posture, image scanning, runtime threat detection and admission control for AKS, EKS and GKE; AWS splits runtime detection (GuardDuty) from image scanning (Inspector).

Both cache upstream registries (ACR artifact cache vs ECR pull-through cache) and replicate images; ACR geo-replication and connected registries need Premium and ACR Tasks builds images, while ECR uses replication rules and relies on CodeBuild for builds.
ACR Tasks builds and patches images inside the registry on commit or base-image update; on AWS you build with CodeBuild and push to ECR.
Both run containers without servers; ACI exposes container groups directly, Fargate always runs inside an ECS task or EKS pod.

pairs.b: AWS App Runner (closed to new customers since 2026-04-30)
pairs.difference: Both are opinionated HTTP container platforms; App Runner no longer accepts new customers and AWS points them to ECS Express Mode.

pairs.b: Amazon ECS on Fargate (including Express Mode)
pairs.difference: Container Apps is Kubernetes-based with KEDA scaling, revisions, Dapr and scale-to-zero; ECS services keep at least the minimum task count you set and expose all generated resources.

pairs.b: ECS scheduled tasks or AWS Batch on Fargate
pairs.difference: Container Apps jobs support manual, scheduled and event-driven triggers natively; ECS uses EventBridge Scheduler to launch tasks.
Functions groups many functions in one app with declarative triggers and bindings; Lambda deploys each function separately and uses event source mappings or service integrations.

Flex Consumption adds always-ready instances and VNet integration to pay-per-use billing, and replaces the Linux Consumption plan retiring 2028-09-30; Lambda's equivalents are provisioned concurrency and SnapStart.

Both checkpoint and replay code-first workflows; Durable Functions runs inside a Functions app with entities and pluggable storage including Durable Task Scheduler, while Lambda durable functions run inside one function, stop billing while waiting, last up to a year and have SDKs for C#, Python, Java, Go, JavaScript and TypeScript.
Durable Functions writes orchestration as code; Step Functions defines state machines in Amazon States Language with visual tooling and direct SDK integrations.

Logic Apps is a connector-rich integration designer with more than 1,400 connectors; Step Functions orchestrates AWS service calls with Standard (up to a year) and Express (up to five minutes) workflows.

pairs.a: Logic Apps connectors and Data Factory
pairs.difference: AppFlow moves data between SaaS apps such as Salesforce or ServiceNow and S3, Redshift or EventBridge on schedules or events; Azure covers this with Logic Apps connectors for operational flows and Data Factory for bulk movement.

pairs.a: Logic Apps HTTP actions and API connections
pairs.difference: API destinations let EventBridge rules call external HTTP APIs with managed authentication and rate limits; Logic Apps calls them from workflow actions.

pairs.a: (no standalone Azure scheduler service; Logic Apps recurrence or Functions timer triggers)
pairs.difference: EventBridge Scheduler is a standalone service that invokes many AWS targets on one-time or recurring schedules at scale; Azure schedules work inside Logic Apps, Functions or Container Apps jobs.

API Management is a full API platform with a developer portal, products, a policy pipeline, workspaces and a self-hosted gateway; API Gateway offers REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs with usage plans and Lambda authorizers.
API Management can run its gateway as a container on-premises or in other clouds under central control; API Gateway runs only inside AWS.
The AI gateway adds token limits, semantic caching and load balancing in front of model and MCP endpoints; AgentCore Gateway turns APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools for agents.

pairs.a: API Management GraphQL APIs and Data API builder
pairs.difference: AppSync is a managed GraphQL service with resolvers, subscriptions and caching; Azure exposes or synthesizes GraphQL through API Management and generates GraphQL and REST over databases with Data API builder.

pairs.a: Azure Web PubSub and Azure SignalR Service
pairs.b: API Gateway WebSocket APIs and AWS AppSync Events
pairs.difference: The Azure services manage connection fan-out and groups (SignalR adds the ASP.NET Core protocol); API Gateway WebSocket APIs route messages to backends, AppSync Events provides pub/sub channels.

pairs.b: AWS AppConfig and Systems Manager Parameter Store
pairs.difference: App Configuration is a key-value store with labels and snapshots; AppConfig deploys configuration with validators and gradual rollouts, Parameter Store holds hierarchical parameters.

Both store flags with targeting and variants that SDKs evaluate in the app; AppConfig rolls flag changes out gradually with automatic rollback on alarms, App Configuration pairs with the .NET Feature Management library.
Both send transactional and bulk email through APIs and SMTP with domain verification and engagement tracking; SES also receives inbound mail.

pairs.b: Amazon SNS mobile push and AWS End User Messaging
pairs.difference: Both fan out push notifications to APNs and FCM; AWS End User Messaging also covers SMS and voice, which Azure handles in Communication Services.
