Service Bus is an AMQP broker with sessions, transactions, scheduled delivery and duplicate detection; SQS is an HTTP-polled queue built on visibility timeouts.
Both are simple, inexpensive HTTP queues with visibility timeouts; Queue Storage lives in a storage account and has no built-in dead-letter queue, SQS adds redrive policies and FIFO variants.

pairs.b: Amazon SNS topic with SQS subscriptions
pairs.difference: Service Bus subscriptions are durable filtered queues inside the broker; SNS pushes without storing, so durable fan-out needs SQS subscribers.
Both give ordered, exclusive processing per key; Service Bus sessions also carry session state.
Service Bus lets you configure the detection window up to seven days; SQS FIFO uses a fixed five-minute window.

pairs.b: SQS dead-letter queue with redrive policy
pairs.difference: Service Bus dead-letter queues are built-in subqueues of every entity; SQS dead-letter queues are separate queues wired up through maxReceiveCount and redrive.
Amazon MQ runs managed open-source ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ brokers; Service Bus supports JMS 2.0 and AMQP on a proprietary broker.
Both route discrete events with filtering; EventBridge adds archive and replay, a schema registry, Pipes and Scheduler.
Both filter on event attributes; EventBridge patterns can match any JSON field with prefix, numeric and anything-but operators.
Pipes connect a source to a target with filtering and enrichment and no code; Azure uses Functions or Logic Apps for the same glue.
Both are managed MQTT brokers with topic routing; IoT Core adds a device registry, shadows and rules for IoT fleets, while the Event Grid broker routes MQTT messages into Event Grid for any client.
Both are partitioned, replayable streams; Event Hubs scales by throughput or processing units, Kinesis by shards or on-demand mode.
Event Hubs speaks the Kafka protocol on its own engine with no brokers to manage; MSK runs real Apache Kafka clusters or MSK Serverless.
Capture writes Avro or Parquet to Blob Storage or ADLS on a time or size window; Firehose delivers to many destinations with transformation and format conversion.

pairs.b: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
pairs.difference: Stream Analytics uses a SQL dialect on a managed engine; Managed Flink runs Apache Flink applications in Java, Python or SQL.
Both store Avro or JSON schemas with compatibility rules for producers and consumers; Glue Schema Registry serves Kinesis, MSK and Flink, Azure Schema Registry lives in an Event Hubs namespace.

pairs.b: Kinesis Data Streams plus Managed Service for Apache Flink
pairs.difference: Real-Time Intelligence is a SaaS eventstream-to-Eventhouse (KQL) suite on Fabric capacity; AWS composes ingestion, processing and storage from separately billed services.
Both provide device identity, MQTT, AMQP or HTTPS ingestion, cloud-to-device messaging and twins or shadows; IoT Core adds a rules engine, IoT Hub routes to Event Hubs, Service Bus and storage.
Both run modules or components on edge devices with offline operation; IoT Edge modules are containers, Greengrass components run native code, containers or Lambda functions.
Both provision devices at scale with X.509 or TPM attestation; DPS is a separate service that assigns devices to hubs, fleet provisioning uses templates inside IoT Core.
Device Defender audits AWS IoT configurations and detects device anomalies; Defender for IoT focuses on agentless monitoring of OT and IoT networks plus device posture.
Both are object stores with tiers, versioning and lifecycle rules; Blob Storage sits inside a storage account that also sets redundancy, network rules and keys.
A storage account is a namespace that sets redundancy, network rules, encryption and access keys for its blobs, files, queues and tables; S3 has no container above the bucket.

pairs.a: Blob access tiers (Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive)
pairs.difference: Azure sets tiers per blob or as an account default with 30, 90 and 180-day minimums for Cool, Cold and Archive; S3 sets classes per object, including Intelligent-Tiering and One Zone-IA.

Both move objects between frequent and infrequent tiers automatically for a per-object monitoring fee with no retrieval or early-deletion charges; smart tier needs a zone-redundant account and never uses Archive, while Intelligent-Tiering adds optional archive access tiers.

Both are online tiers for rarely read data with millisecond access, higher read charges and a 90-day minimum; Cold follows the account's redundancy setting, Glacier Instant Retrieval stores across multiple AZs.

pairs.b: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Glacier Deep Archive
pairs.difference: Both are offline tiers needing hours to rehydrate or restore; Archive works only in LRS, GRS and RA-GRS accounts and can take up to 15 hours, while the Glacier classes store data across multiple AZs.
Both keep prior versions on overwrite and delete; S3 versioning can only be suspended once enabled, Azure versioning can be disabled, and both pair with lifecycle rules to expire old versions.

pairs.b: S3 Versioning delete markers plus MFA Delete
pairs.difference: Soft delete keeps deleted blobs or containers for a set number of days and can undelete them; S3 has no soft delete, so recovery relies on versioning delete markers, with MFA Delete protecting version deletion.
Both provide WORM; Object Lock has governance and compliance modes per object version, Azure applies policies at container or version level.
Both copy objects asynchronously by rule; S3 Replication Time Control adds a 15-minute replication SLA.
GRS replicates the whole account to the paired region automatically; CRR is configured per bucket to any Region you choose.
Both replicate synchronously across zones; S3 Standard always stores data across at least three AZs, while ZRS is an option you choose per account.
Both grant time-limited delegated access; a user delegation SAS is signed with Entra credentials, much like a presigned URL signed by an IAM principal.
A stored access policy lets you change or revoke a group of service SAS tokens server-side; a presigned URL can't be revoked except by removing the signer's permissions or waiting for expiry.
Storage accounts have two account-wide keys granting full data access; S3 has no bucket keys, and AWS access keys belong to IAM principals.
Both are account-level switches that override container or bucket settings to prevent public reads; Block Public Access can also be enforced organization-wide.

pairs.a: Storage firewall and virtual network rules
pairs.b: Bucket-policy conditions on aws:SourceVpce and aws:SourceIp
pairs.difference: Azure filters network access to the whole storage account with IP and VNet rules plus resource-instance exceptions; S3 expresses network restrictions as conditions in bucket or endpoint policies.

pairs.a: Encryption scopes, customer-managed keys and infrastructure encryption
pairs.b: SSE-KMS defaults, DSSE-KMS and S3 Bucket Keys
pairs.difference: Azure always encrypts and lets you add customer-managed keys per account or encryption scope plus double encryption; S3 encrypts with SSE-S3 by default and lets you choose SSE-KMS, dual-layer DSSE-KMS and Bucket Keys per bucket or object.
Requester Pays bills the downloader for requests and transfer; Azure always bills the storage account owner.
Access points give a bucket many named endpoints, each with its own policy and optional VPC restriction; Azure uses SAS, RBAC conditions or separate containers instead.
Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through CloudFront edge locations to a bucket; Blob Storage has no edge-accelerated upload.
Both produce scheduled CSV or Parquet reports of objects and their properties.

Storage Lens gives organization-wide usage and activity metrics with recommendations; Storage insights shows capacity, performance and availability per account (check whether Azure Storage Discovery is GA as the closer estate-wide view).

pairs.b: S3 with Lake Formation, or S3 directory buckets
pairs.difference: Hierarchical namespace gives real directories with atomic renames and POSIX ACLs; S3 general-purpose buckets are flat, with Lake Formation adding table-level permissions.
Blob SFTP is a protocol endpoint on a storage account with local users; Transfer Family is a managed SFTP, FTPS, FTP and AS2 service in front of S3 or EFS with IdP integration.
File Sync caches Azure file shares on Windows Servers with cloud tiering; S3 File Gateway presents S3 buckets over SMB or NFS from a VM or appliance.

pairs.b: Storage Gateway Volume Gateway and Tape Gateway
pairs.difference: Volume Gateway presents iSCSI block volumes backed by S3 snapshots and Tape Gateway a virtual tape library; Azure retired StorSimple in 2022 without a replacement.
Both move file data online through agents; DataSync also moves between AWS storage services and from other clouds.

pairs.b: AWS Snowball Edge (closed to new customers since 2025-11-07) or AWS Data Transfer Terminal
pairs.difference: Data Box ships offline transfer appliances; AWS no longer offers Snowball Edge to new customers and points them to DataSync or Data Transfer Terminal.

pairs.b: AWS CLI s3 cp and sync
pairs.difference: Both copy and sync large data sets with parallelism and resume; AzCopy can also copy server-side from S3 into Blob Storage.
Storage Explorer is a desktop GUI for blobs, files, queues, tables and ADLS; AWS offers the S3 console and CLI, with desktop clients from third parties.
Both are network block storage with incremental snapshots; Azure also offers zone-redundant disks, while EBS volumes are always single-AZ.

pairs.b: (no AWS equivalent; EBS volumes live in one AZ)
pairs.difference: ZRS disks replicate synchronously across three zones and can be attached to a VM in another zone after a zone failure; on AWS you rebuild from snapshots or replicate at the application layer.

pairs.a: Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk
pairs.difference: All four let you set IOPS and throughput separately from size; Ultra and io2 Block Express target sub-millisecond, high-IOPS databases, Premium SSD v2 and gp3 are the general-purpose tunable tiers.
Both let clustered apps attach one volume to several VMs; Multi-Attach works only for io1 and io2 volumes in one AZ, shared disks support several disk types, including ZRS disks across zones.
Elastic SAN is a pooled iSCSI SAN you carve into volumes for VMs and AKS; AWS offers per-volume EBS only.

pairs.b: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
pairs.difference: Both offer managed SMB with AD integration; Azure Files provides serverless shares in a storage account, FSx deploys a Windows file system with provisioned throughput.
EFS is elastic NFS with no capacity provisioning; Azure Files NFS shares need the premium SSD file share tier.
Both are built on NetApp ONTAP with snapshots and replication; Azure NetApp Files is a first-party service with capacity pools, FSx for ONTAP exposes ONTAP's own management interfaces.
Both are managed Lustre file systems that integrate with object storage (Blob or S3) for HPC and AI training.
FSx for OpenZFS offers ZFS-based NFS file systems with snapshots and clones; Azure has no managed ZFS service.

pairs.a: Azure Files snapshots and soft delete
pairs.b: FSx shadow copies and AWS Backup
pairs.difference: Azure Files takes share snapshots and keeps deleted shares under soft delete; FSx for Windows exposes Windows shadow copies to users and relies on backups for recovery.
Cosmos DB bills request units and offers five consistency levels; DynamoDB bills read and write capacity units with per-read eventual or strong consistency.

pairs.b: DynamoDB read consistency and global-table modes
pairs.difference: Cosmos DB offers Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix and Eventual; DynamoDB offers strong or eventual reads plus MREC or MRSC modes for global tables.
Both replicate active-active; DynamoDB's MRSC mode adds synchronous strong consistency across exactly three Regions but drops TTL, LSIs and transactions.
Both expose ordered item changes; DynamoDB Streams keeps records for 24 hours, the change feed is read from the container itself.
Both bill per request; Cosmos DB serverless accounts are limited to one region.
The integrated cache is an item and query cache in Cosmos DB's dedicated gateway; DAX is a separate in-memory cluster in your VPC with microsecond reads for DynamoDB-compatible calls.

pairs.a: Azure Table Storage and Cosmos DB for Table
pairs.difference: Table Storage is a cheap key-attribute store in a storage account and Cosmos DB for Table adds global distribution under the same API; DynamoDB is richer, with secondary indexes, transactions and streams.

pairs.a: Azure DocumentDB (formerly: Cosmos DB for MongoDB vCore)
pairs.difference: Both are MongoDB-compatible; Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine, Amazon DocumentDB is AWS-proprietary.

pairs.a: Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra or Managed Instance for Apache Cassandra
pairs.difference: Keyspaces is serverless and Cassandra-compatible; Managed Instance runs real Cassandra nodes that you size.
Neptune is a dedicated graph database supporting Gremlin, openCypher and SPARQL, plus Neptune Analytics; Cosmos DB for Gremlin exposes a Gremlin API over Cosmos DB's partitioned store.

pairs.b: Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB or Timestream for LiveAnalytics
pairs.difference: Azure Data Explorer is a KQL analytics engine for logs and time series at scale; Timestream offers managed InfluxDB or a serverless time-series store (verify LiveAnalytics availability to new customers).

pairs.a: (no first-party OpenSearch on Azure; Elastic Cloud on Azure or Azure AI Search)
pairs.difference: OpenSearch Service runs managed clusters or serverless collections for search, logs and vectors; Azure offers Elastic Cloud as a partner service and AI Search for application search, neither OpenSearch-compatible.
Azure SQL Database is a versionless, database-scoped PaaS with elastic pools, Hyperscale and serverless; RDS runs a specific SQL Server version on an instance you size.

pairs.b: RDS for SQL Server or RDS Custom for SQL Server
pairs.difference: Both give instance-level SQL Server; RDS Custom adds OS access, Managed Instance offers near-full engine compatibility without it.

pairs.a: SQL Server on Azure VMs with the SQL IaaS Agent extension
pairs.difference: Same engine on IaaS; the SQL IaaS Agent extension adds portal management, automated patching and backup, license-type changes and Azure Hybrid Benefit, while on EC2 you manage SQL Server yourself or with Systems Manager.
Both separate compute from distributed log-structured storage; Hyperscale runs SQL Server, Aurora runs MySQL or PostgreSQL.
Both autoscale compute; AWS has no serverless SQL Server engine.

pairs.a: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server
pairs.b: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL or Aurora PostgreSQL
pairs.difference: Flexible server maps closely to RDS; Aurora's shared-storage design is closest to Azure HorizonDB, which is still in preview.

pairs.a: Azure Database for MySQL flexible server
pairs.b: Amazon RDS for MySQL and Aurora MySQL
pairs.difference: Flexible server maps closely to RDS for MySQL; Aurora MySQL's shared distributed storage has no GA Azure MySQL counterpart.
Aurora DSQL is a serverless, active-active multi-Region PostgreSQL-compatible database; Azure has no GA distributed SQL service with that model.
Both run Oracle Exadata and Autonomous Database services operated by Oracle inside the provider's datacenters and billed through the marketplace; regional availability and integrations differ.

Both keep synchronous replicas in other zones with automatic failover; zone redundancy is a setting on the database or pool, RDS Multi-AZ adds a standby or, in Multi-AZ DB clusters, two readable standbys.

pairs.b: Aurora Global Database and RDS cross-Region read replicas
pairs.difference: Failover groups replicate databases asynchronously to another region behind listener endpoints that survive failover; Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer with managed switchover, and RDS cross-Region replicas are promoted manually.

pairs.a: Read scale-out and Hyperscale named replicas
pairs.b: RDS read replicas and Aurora Replicas
pairs.difference: Both offload reads to replicas with their own endpoints; Aurora Replicas share the cluster volume, Azure SQL read scale-out uses the HA replica and Hyperscale named replicas scale independently.

pairs.a: Point-in-time restore, long-term retention and geo-restore
pairs.difference: Both restore to any point in a retention window and keep long-term copies; Azure SQL geo-restore uses geo-replicated backups, RDS copies snapshots or replicates automated backups to another Region.

pairs.a: Built-in PgBouncer on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server
pairs.difference: RDS Proxy is a managed, multi-AZ connection pooler with IAM authentication and faster failover for RDS and Aurora; PgBouncer is an option on PostgreSQL flexible server only, and Azure SQL has no proxy equivalent.

pairs.b: AWS Schema Conversion Tool and DMS Schema Conversion
pairs.difference: Both assess and convert schemas from Oracle, Db2 and other engines; SSMA targets SQL Server and Azure SQL, SCT and DMS Schema Conversion target Aurora, RDS and Redshift.
Azure Managed Redis runs Redis Inc. software and replaces Azure Cache for Redis (retiring 2027–2028); ElastiCache offers Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached, node-based or serverless.
MemoryDB is a durable primary database with a multi-AZ transaction log; Azure Managed Redis offers persistence and active geo-replication but is positioned as a cache.
Both run vector similarity search inside the in-memory engine for low-latency semantic caching and retrieval.

pairs.a: Cosmos DB for NoSQL vector search
pairs.b: Amazon DocumentDB vector search or DynamoDB zero-ETL integration with OpenSearch Service
pairs.difference: Cosmos DB stores vectors next to operational documents with DiskANN, quantized-flat and flat indexes plus hybrid full-text ranking; DynamoDB has no native vector index, so AWS uses DocumentDB vector search or replicates DynamoDB into OpenSearch.
S3 Vectors is low-cost vector storage in S3 (GA December 2025); Azure AI Search keeps vectors in a search index alongside text for hybrid queries.
Both provide full-text, vector and hybrid search; Azure AI Search adds indexers, AI enrichment skillsets and agentic retrieval as a managed service.

pairs.b: S3 with Lake Formation and the Glue Data Catalog
pairs.difference: Fabric is a SaaS suite on one tenant-wide lake with capacity billing; AWS composes separately billed services inside your accounts.

pairs.a: Fabric Warehouse or Synapse dedicated SQL pool
pairs.difference: Both are MPP warehouses; Redshift offers provisioned and Serverless, Fabric Warehouse runs on shared Fabric capacity.

pairs.a: Azure Data Factory (and Fabric Data Factory)
pairs.b: AWS Glue ETL and Amazon MWAA
pairs.difference: Data Factory is a low-code orchestration and copy service with mapping data flows; AWS splits Spark-based ETL (Glue) from Airflow orchestration (MWAA).

pairs.b: Amazon EMR or Databricks on AWS
pairs.difference: Azure Databricks is a first-party service sold and supported by Microsoft; on AWS, EMR is the native managed Spark and Hadoop service and Databricks is a partner deployment in your account.

pairs.a: Synapse serverless SQL pool or Fabric SQL analytics endpoint
pairs.difference: All query lake files with SQL; Athena is serverless Trino billed per TB scanned or provisioned capacity, the Fabric endpoint runs on Fabric capacity over Delta tables.

pairs.b: Amazon SageMaker Catalog and AWS Glue Data Catalog
pairs.difference: Purview catalogs and governs data across Azure, Fabric, on-premises and other clouds with a business glossary and data quality; Glue Data Catalog is the technical metastore for AWS analytics and SageMaker Catalog adds business publishing and subscription.

pairs.b: Amazon Quick Sight (a feature of Amazon Quick; formerly: Amazon QuickSight)
pairs.difference: Both are BI services with dashboards, embedding and natural-language Q&A; Quick Sight is now a feature of Amazon Quick (SAA-C03 says Amazon Quick, SAP-C02 still says QuickSight), Power BI is part of Microsoft Fabric.

pairs.a: Microsoft Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365 Copilot
pairs.difference: Both bring agents, automation and grounded chat to business users over enterprise data; Copilot Studio publishes agents into Microsoft 365 and Teams, Amazon Quick bundles agents, flows, research and Quick Sight in one AWS-hosted SaaS.
Both collect metrics, logs and alerts; Azure Monitor routes logs into Log Analytics workspaces, CloudWatch keeps metrics and log groups per account and Region.
A workspace is a cross-resource store of typed tables queried with KQL; log groups are per-source streams queried with Logs Insights.
KQL is a full analytics language shared with Sentinel and Azure Data Explorer; Logs Insights also accepts OpenSearch PPL and SQL.

pairs.a: Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules
pairs.b: CloudWatch agent with configuration in Parameter Store
pairs.difference: AMA uses data collection rules associated with machines, including Arc servers, to choose what to collect and where; the CloudWatch agent reads a JSON configuration, often distributed through Parameter Store.

pairs.b: Service-vended logs to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose
pairs.difference: Azure exposes one diagnostic-settings mechanism on nearly every resource; AWS configures log delivery separately for each service.

pairs.a: Diagnostic settings streaming to Event Hubs
pairs.b: CloudWatch Logs subscription filters to Kinesis or Firehose
pairs.difference: Both stream logs in near real time to a pipeline for SIEMs or other tools; Azure streams per resource or workspace export, AWS per log group or account-level filter.
Both trade query features for cheaper ingestion of high-volume logs; Azure plans are set per table, the Infrequent Access class per log group.
Action groups are reusable notification and automation bundles; CloudWatch alarm actions target SNS, Auto Scaling, EC2 or Systems Manager.
Alert processing rules suppress or reroute notifications by scope and schedule, such as maintenance windows; CloudWatch suppresses composite alarm actions with a suppressor alarm.
Both collect performance data, logs and maps for VMs and Kubernetes; VM insights also covers Arc servers, CloudWatch Container Insights covers EKS, ECS and Kubernetes on EC2.

pairs.a: Azure Workbooks and dashboards with Grafana
pairs.difference: Both build interactive operational dashboards; Workbooks mix KQL, metrics and parameters in one report, CloudWatch dashboards can span accounts and Regions.
Both record control-plane operations for 90 days by default; the activity log is per subscription, CloudTrail event history per account and Region, with longer retention through export or trails.

pairs.a: Microsoft Entra sign-in and audit logs
pairs.b: CloudTrail sign-in events and IAM Identity Center events
pairs.difference: Entra logs interactive, non-interactive, service-principal and managed-identity sign-ins with Conditional Access results; CloudTrail records console and Identity Center sign-ins and API calls but not sign-ins to third-party apps.

pairs.a: Diagnostic settings to a central Log Analytics workspace
pairs.b: CloudTrail organization trail to a log archive account
pairs.difference: AWS centralises audit logs with an organization trail into S3 in a dedicated account; Azure centralises with policy-driven diagnostic settings into a shared workspace.

pairs.b: CloudWatch Application Signals with AWS X-Ray
pairs.difference: Both provide APM with traces, dependency maps and SLOs; Application Insights stores telemetry in Log Analytics, Application Signals builds on X-Ray traces and CloudWatch metrics.
Both probe endpoints from provider locations; Synthetics canaries are Node.js or Python scripts, Application Insights standard tests are configured pings with TLS and content checks.
Both collect real-user page loads, errors and sessions from the browser with a JavaScript snippet.
Both package OpenTelemetry for their backend; the X-Ray SDKs and daemon reach end of support on February 25, 2027 in favour of OpenTelemetry.

pairs.a: Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus
pairs.difference: Both are managed Prometheus-compatible stores; Azure ties scraping to AKS and Arc clusters through the Azure Monitor agent.
Both run managed Grafana workspaces with provider data sources and SSO (Entra ID vs IAM Identity Center or SAML).

pairs.b: AWS Security Hub, GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie
pairs.difference: Defender for Cloud is one CNAPP with posture management plus per-resource protection plans; AWS ships separate services that the new Security Hub correlates.
Both run continuous best-practice checks; Security Hub CSPM is the renamed original Security Hub using ASFF, while the new Security Hub uses OCSF.
Both correlate misconfigurations, vulnerabilities and reachability into prioritised exposure paths.

pairs.b: GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring with Inspector EC2 scanning
pairs.difference: Defender for Servers includes Microsoft Defender for Endpoint EDR; AWS has no first-party EDR agent.
Both scan new uploads for malware and tag or report results, billed per GB scanned; Defender for Storage also detects anomalous access.
Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 only; Defender CSPM discovers it across Azure storage and databases and AWS S3 and RDS and feeds it into attack paths.
Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 only; Purview labels and protects data across Microsoft 365, Azure and other clouds.

pairs.b: GuardDuty detections on CloudTrail management events
pairs.difference: Both detect suspicious control-plane activity; GuardDuty analyses CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs as foundational sources, Defender for Resource Manager watches Resource Manager operations.
RDS Protection detects anomalous logins on Aurora and RDS; Defender for Databases covers Azure SQL, open-source databases and Cosmos DB with vulnerability assessment and threat detection.

pairs.a: Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management
pairs.difference: EASM discovers your internet-facing assets from the outside, beyond Azure; AWS tools only analyse resources inside your accounts.
Sentinel is a SIEM with SOAR, analytics rules and UEBA; Security Lake normalises security data into OCSF in your S3 for other tools to analyse.

pairs.b: OpenSearch Service security analytics or a partner SIEM
pairs.difference: AWS has no first-party SIEM, so OpenSearch security analytics or partners fill the role Sentinel plays on Azure.

pairs.b: Security Hub automation rules with EventBridge and Systems Manager Automation
pairs.difference: Sentinel triggers Logic Apps playbooks from incidents and alerts; AWS updates findings with automation rules and routes them through EventBridge to Lambda, Step Functions or Systems Manager Automation.

pairs.a: Sentinel investigation graph and Defender XDR incidents
pairs.difference: Detective builds behaviour graphs from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, GuardDuty and EKS audit logs; Defender XDR and Sentinel correlate alerts across identity, endpoint, email and cloud into incidents with graph views.
Defender for Cloud and Sentinel onboard AWS accounts natively; AWS security services don't assess Azure resources.

pairs.b: AWS KMS, Secrets Manager and ACM
pairs.difference: Key Vault stores keys, secrets and certificates in one vault; AWS splits them across KMS, Secrets Manager and ACM with Private CA. Rated Azure to AWS; in the reverse direction KMS maps closely to Key Vault keys.
Both back envelope encryption for platform services; every KMS key has a mandatory key policy, Key Vault keys are governed by Azure RBAC and can be HSM-protected in the Premium tier.
Both rotate key material on a schedule while keeping old versions for decryption; KMS supports 90 to 2,560-day periods and on-demand rotation, Key Vault rotation policies also notify before expiry.
Secrets Manager has built-in Lambda-driven rotation; Key Vault secret rotation relies on near-expiry Event Grid events and your own function.
ACM issues public certificates that auto-renew on integrated services; Key Vault manages certificate lifecycles with partner CAs and stores them alongside secrets.

pairs.a: (no first-party Azure managed private CA; Microsoft Cloud PKI covers Intune-managed devices only)
pairs.difference: Private CA issues and manages private certificate hierarchies as a service; Key Vault can request certificates from integrated CAs or self-sign but doesn't operate a private CA.

pairs.b: AWS CloudHSM or KMS custom key store
pairs.difference: Managed HSM is a single-tenant FIPS 140-3 Level 3 key pool behind Key Vault APIs; CloudHSM gives raw HSM access that can also back KMS keys.

Both give single-tenant HSM clusters you administer with vendor tools; Azure Cloud HSM is IaaS-only and can't hold customer-managed keys for PaaS services, which use Managed HSM, and it succeeds Dedicated HSM (supported until 2028-07-31).
Payment HSM gives you dedicated payment HSMs to operate; Payment Cryptography is a serverless API for payment key management and PIN, card and MAC operations.
KMS access starts from the key's resource policy; Key Vault access comes from Azure RBAC role assignments, with access policies now a legacy model.
Bicep is a DSL transpiled to ARM JSON and deployed by Resource Manager; CloudFormation processes templates into stacks that own their resources.
The CDK synthesises CloudFormation from general-purpose languages such as C#, Python and TypeScript; Bicep is a declarative DSL with modules.
An ARM deployment is a historical record that doesn't own resources; a stack owns its resources and rolls back on failure.
Deployment stacks add managed-resource tracking, deny settings and delete-on-unmanage to ARM; CloudFormation adds stack policies, DeletionPolicy and drift detection.
Both preview changes before deploying; a change set is a stored object you execute later.

pairs.b: CloudFormation modules or Service Catalog products
pairs.difference: Template specs store versioned templates as Azure resources shared with RBAC; CloudFormation modules package reusable resource fragments in the registry, and Service Catalog shares approved products.
Deployment scripts run Azure CLI or PowerShell in a temporary container during a deployment; custom resources invoke a Lambda function you write to handle create, update and delete.
AVM are Microsoft-supported Bicep and Terraform modules following one specification; CDK constructs are code libraries in C#, Python and other languages.

pairs.b: CloudFormation IaC generator and cdk migrate
pairs.difference: Both turn existing resources into templates; the IaC generator scans an account and creates an importable stack template, Azure exports one resource group or resource at a time.

pairs.a: PSRule for Azure and the Bicep linter
pairs.difference: Both lint templates and test them against best-practice or policy rules in CI before deployment.

pairs.a: Azure Policy evaluated at Resource Manager request time
pairs.difference: Azure Policy evaluates every Resource Manager write whatever tool sends it; Hooks inspect only resources deployed through CloudFormation or Cloud Control API.
Both are first-class providers; azurerm depends on resource-provider registration in each subscription, the aws provider is configured per Region and account.
Both are thin providers generated from the platform's resource schemas (Resource Manager REST API vs Cloud Control API) that expose new resource types quickly.

pairs.a: Terraform state in Azure Blob Storage (lease locking)
pairs.difference: Both use the cloud's object store; the S3 backend now locks with use_lockfile, and DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated.

pairs.a: GitHub Actions OIDC to an Entra federated credential
pairs.b: GitHub Actions OIDC to an IAM role
pairs.difference: Both remove stored secrets; Entra matches issuer and subject on an app or managed identity, AWS matches token claims in the role trust policy.
Azure Pipelines is one YAML pipeline engine with hosted agents; AWS separates orchestration (CodePipeline) from build execution (CodeBuild).

pairs.a: Azure Pipelines agents and GitHub-hosted runners
pairs.b: CodeBuild compute and self-hosted GitHub Actions runners on CodeBuild
pairs.difference: Azure DevOps and GitHub offer hosted and self-hosted agents; CodeBuild provides on-demand build containers or reserved fleets and can also host GitHub Actions runners.

Both host Git repositories with pull requests and branch policies; Azure Repos sits inside Azure DevOps with Boards and Pipelines, CodeCommit is a standalone, IAM-authenticated service with fewer collaboration features.
Azure Boards and GitHub Projects track work items, sprints and flow metrics; AWS has no work-tracking service, so teams use Jira or GitHub.
Both host NuGet, npm, Maven and PyPI feeds with upstream sources; Azure Artifacts adds feed views for promotion, CodeArtifact uses domains to share packages across accounts.
Both pause a release for human or automated gates; Azure environments add checks such as business hours, Azure Monitor alerts and exclusive locks.

pairs.a: Deployment slot swaps and rolling or canary pipeline strategies
pairs.difference: CodeDeploy implements in-place, blue/green, canary and linear deployments with automatic rollback for EC2, ECS and Lambda; Azure gets the same strategies from slots, Container Apps revisions, scale set rolling upgrades or pipeline deployment jobs.

pairs.b: AWS Cost Explorer and Billing and Cost Management
pairs.difference: Both analyse cost by scope and tag; Cost Management scopes follow billing accounts and the management-group hierarchy, Cost Explorer follows the organization's accounts.
Both alert on thresholds; AWS Budget actions can apply SCPs or IAM policies automatically, Azure budgets trigger action groups.
Both use machine learning to flag unusual spend and notify; Cost Anomaly Detection monitors by service, account, cost category or tag.
Both export detailed usage, including the FinOps FOCUS schema, into object storage for analysis.

pairs.b: AWS Cost Categories and split cost allocation data
pairs.difference: Azure cost allocation rules redistribute shared costs among subscriptions or tags; Cost Categories group costs by rules and split cost allocation data apportions EC2 costs to ECS tasks and EKS pods.
Both estimate monthly costs for a configured architecture; the AWS calculator in the console can also apply your discounts and commitments.
Both build a TCO-style business case from discovered on-premises inventory; Migration Evaluator is an AWS-assisted program, the business case is self-service in Azure Migrate.
Both discount one- or three-year commitments to specific resource types; EC2 Standard RIs can also be sold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace.

pairs.b: Convertible RIs and the Reserved Instance Marketplace
pairs.difference: Azure lets you exchange reservations and refund up to an annual limit; AWS lets you exchange Convertible RIs and sell Standard EC2 RIs on the Marketplace.
Both commit to hourly spend across compute services; Azure's covers VMs, App Service, Functions Premium and container services, AWS's covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda.
Database Savings Plans apply one spend commitment across Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache and other database services; Azure database discounts are per-service reservations.

pairs.b: Bring your own license with AWS License Manager
pairs.difference: Hybrid Benefit discounts Windows Server and SQL Server with Software Assurance on shared hardware; on AWS, Windows Server BYOL generally needs Dedicated Hosts.
Azure Dev/Test subscriptions remove Windows and SQL Server license charges and discount some services for Visual Studio subscribers; AWS has no dev/test price list.

pairs.a: Microsoft Customer Agreement billing account, profiles and invoice sections
pairs.b: AWS Organizations consolidated billing and Billing Conductor
pairs.difference: Azure's billing hierarchy is separate from its resource hierarchy; AWS ties billing to the organization's management account.
Both sell tiered support with response-time targets; AWS ties the full Trusted Advisor checks and other features to higher plans (check current tier names on both).

pairs.b: AWS Compute Optimizer and Cost Optimization Hub
pairs.difference: Advisor gives rightsizing, idle-resource and reservation advice in one list; AWS uses Compute Optimizer for rightsizing and Cost Optimization Hub to consolidate savings opportunities across accounts.

pairs.a: Data transfer between availability zones in a region (free on Azure)
pairs.b: Cross-AZ data transfer (billed per GB in each direction)
pairs.difference: Azure doesn't charge for transfer between zones in a region, over private or public IPs; AWS bills most cross-AZ traffic per GB each way, which changes the cost of multi-AZ designs.
Azure charges VNet peering per GB in both directions even within a region; VPC peering has no peering charge, with same-AZ traffic free and cross-AZ traffic at the standard inter-AZ rate.
Both centralise backup policies across services; AWS Backup copies across accounts within an organization, Azure Backup across regions and subscriptions.

pairs.a: Recovery Services vault and Backup vault
pairs.difference: Azure has two vault types for different workloads; AWS has one vault type plus logically air-gapped vaults.
Both make recovery points undeletable before expiry, even by administrators, once locked; Vault Lock also has a governance mode that privileged users can override.

pairs.b: Multi-party approval for logically air-gapped vaults
pairs.difference: Multi-user authorization gates destructive vault operations through a Resource Guard owned in another subscription or tenant; multi-party approval lets an approval team in a separate recovery organization grant restore access to a logically air-gapped vault.

pairs.a: Azure Business Continuity Center and backup reports
pairs.difference: Both report backup coverage and compliance against policies across subscriptions or accounts; Business Continuity Center also covers Site Recovery protection.

pairs.a: Azure Blob operational and vaulted backup
pairs.difference: Both protect object data with continuous point-in-time and periodic backups; operational backup keeps data in the source account, vaulted backup copies it out.
Both replicate servers continuously and orchestrate failover; Site Recovery also replicates Azure VMs between Azure regions.

pairs.a: Azure Site Recovery recovery plans plus Front Door or Traffic Manager failover
pairs.b: Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) (formerly: Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller)
pairs.difference: ARC adds readiness checks, routing controls and Region switch plans to orchestrate multi-Region failover; Azure composes the same from ASR recovery plans and DNS or Front Door failover, with no dedicated recovery-orchestration service.

pairs.a: (no Azure equivalent; Azure fails over zone-redundant services automatically)
pairs.b: ARC zonal shift and zonal autoshift
pairs.difference: Zonal shift lets you, or AWS automatically, move load balancer and EKS traffic away from an impaired AZ; Azure relies on platform-managed failover for zone-redundant services.
Both run managed fault experiments with provider-defined faults and stop conditions; FIS scenarios include AZ power interruption and cross-Region connectivity faults.

pairs.b: AWS Transform with AWS Application Migration Service
pairs.difference: Azure Migrate is one hub for discovery, assessment and migration; AWS Transform, the successor to Migration Hub (closed to new customers since 2025-11-07), handles assessment and modernisation while MGN rehosts servers.

pairs.b: AWS Transform discovery and planning (AWS Application Discovery Service is closed to new customers)
pairs.difference: Azure Migrate discovers VMware, Hyper-V and physical servers with an appliance and produces readiness, sizing and cost assessments; AWS now directs new customers from Application Discovery Service to AWS Transform.
Both replicate servers at block level for lift-and-shift cutover with test failovers.
Both migrate databases online with change data capture; AWS DMS adds DMS Schema Conversion for heterogeneous moves.

pairs.a: GitHub Copilot modernization (formerly: GitHub Copilot app modernization)
pairs.difference: Copilot modernization upgrades code and moves its dependencies to Azure services from the IDE or CLI; AWS Transform for .NET ports .NET Framework apps to cross-platform .NET on Linux on AWS.

Repurchase maps to Replace, and Relocate (to VMware Cloud on AWS or Amazon EVS) maps to Rehost onto Azure VMware Solution; AWS's single Refactor strategy splits into CAF's Refactor, Rearchitect and Rebuild.
Both are managed platforms for models, agents, evaluation and guardrails; Foundry also absorbs Azure OpenAI and Foundry Tools (formerly: Azure AI Services) into one resource with projects.
Both host first- and third-party models, including Anthropic Claude and open-weight models; Foundry includes Azure OpenAI's GPT models, Bedrock includes Amazon Nova.
Both reserve model capacity for predictable latency and cost; units and commitment terms differ.
Both route inference across regions, within a geography or globally, to raise available capacity.
Both process large asynchronous job files at a discount to on-demand prices within a completion window; supported models differ.
Both fine-tune selected first- and third-party models and host the results; supported models and techniques differ, and Bedrock often needs Provisioned Throughput to serve custom models.

pairs.a: Foundry agent versioning and prompts kept in Git
pairs.difference: Bedrock Prompt Management stores versioned prompts with variants as resources; Foundry versions agents automatically and treats prompts as code or project assets.

pairs.a: Azure AI Content Safety and Foundry guardrails
pairs.difference: Both filter harmful content, detect prompt attacks, block listed terms and topics, and check grounding; Bedrock adds Automated Reasoning checks and code-domain filtering, Azure adds protected-material detection, Prompt Shields for indirect attacks in documents, and guardrails per model or agent deployment.

Both run built-in and custom quality and safety evaluators, including LLM-as-judge, on datasets and traces; AWS separates model and knowledge-base evaluations (Bedrock) from agent evaluations (AgentCore).
Both capture OpenTelemetry traces of model and tool calls with dashboards for latency, tokens and errors; Foundry stores them in Application Insights, AgentCore in CloudWatch.

Foundry Agent Service runs prompt, voice-based (preview) and hosted agents behind one service with toolboxes; AgentCore is a set of modular services (Harness, Runtime, Gateway, Memory, Identity, Code Interpreter, Browser, Observability, Evaluations, Optimization, Policy, Registry, Payments) for agents built with any framework.
Both are declarative managed agents configured with instructions, tools and knowledge; neither requires you to host code.

Both run a managed agent loop from a declared model, instructions and tools; Harness runs each session in an isolated microVM with filesystem and shell access and accepts non-Bedrock models, prompt agents run on Foundry's runtime with platform tools.

Both host your containerized agent code with a managed endpoint, session isolation, scaling and an agent identity; hosted agents also accept a .zip that Foundry builds, AgentCore Runtime supports long-running asynchronous sessions.

Both expose curated tools to agents through one MCP endpoint with central authentication; Gateway also converts OpenAPI specs and Lambda functions into tools, toolboxes version tool sets for sharing across agents.
Both give agents short- and long-term memory; AgentCore Memory is a standalone service usable from any framework, Foundry memory is a built-in agent tool (check its GA status).

pairs.a: Foundry code interpreter and Container Apps dynamic sessions
pairs.difference: All run model-generated code in isolated sandboxes; AgentCore Code Interpreter and dynamic sessions can be called from any framework, Foundry's code interpreter is an agent tool.
AgentCore Browser is a managed cloud browser runtime for Playwright or Browser Use; Foundry offers browser automation as an agent tool (check its GA status).
Both use traces and evaluations to propose better instructions and tool descriptions; AgentCore adds A/B traffic splitting through Gateway, the Foundry optimizer is in preview.

pairs.a: (no Azure equivalent; nearest are API Management AI gateway policies and Foundry guardrails)
pairs.difference: AgentCore Policy enforces deterministic rules on every tool call at the Gateway, written in natural language or a Cedar-compatible language; Azure has no policy engine dedicated to agent tool calls.

Both catalog agents and tools for discovery and governance; Entra Agent Registry sits in the directory next to agent identities, AgentCore Registry adds publish, review and approve workflows with semantic search.
AgentCore Payments lets agents pay for APIs and content through x402 and the Machine Payments Protocol with wallets and spending limits; Azure has no first-party agent payment service.
Both let agents call each other over the A2A protocol; Foundry's A2A v1.0 endpoint is GA with v0.3 in preview, AgentCore Runtime hosts A2A servers.
Both are open-source agent SDKs; Agent Framework succeeds Semantic Kernel and AutoGen and runs on Foundry hosted agents, Strands pairs with AgentCore Runtime.
Both are managed RAG layers; Foundry IQ is built on Azure AI Search agentic retrieval, Bedrock Knowledge Bases sit on a vector store such as OpenSearch Serverless or S3 Vectors.
Both are managed enterprise search with connectors and semantic ranking; Kendra no longer accepts new customers and AWS points them to Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
Both cover training, pipelines, registries and managed endpoints; SageMaker AI adds HyperPod for resilient large-scale distributed training.
Both version models with stages or approval status for promotion; Azure ML registries also share environments, components and data across workspaces and regions.
Both host models behind autoscaling HTTPS endpoints with traffic splitting for safe rollout; SageMaker adds serverless and asynchronous inference options.
Both orchestrate ML steps as DAGs with caching and lineage; Azure ML pipelines are built from reusable components, SageMaker Pipelines from steps defined in the Python SDK.
Both detect data drift and quality degradation on deployed models and raise alerts; Model Monitor schedules jobs against data captured from endpoints.
Both explain models and assess fairness; Clarify also detects bias in training data and evaluates foundation models, the dashboard adds error analysis and counterfactuals.

pairs.a: Azure ML distributed training on compute clusters
pairs.difference: HyperPod provides self-healing clusters for multi-week foundation-model training; Azure ML runs distributed jobs on compute clusters, with very large training otherwise on CycleCloud or AKS GPU clusters.
Both analyse images and video and detect faces; Face identification and verification on Azure need limited-access approval.
Azure combines speech-to-text, text-to-speech and speech translation in one service; AWS splits them across services.
Both provide entity recognition, sentiment, PII detection and custom classification.
Both translate text and documents with custom terminology; Translator also offers custom-trained models.

pairs.a: Azure Document Intelligence in Foundry Tools
pairs.difference: Both extract text, tables and fields from documents with prebuilt and custom models.

pairs.a: Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools
pairs.difference: Both extract structured output from documents, images, audio and video with generative models, configured as analyzers or blueprints.

pairs.a: Conversational language understanding or Copilot Studio
pairs.difference: Lex builds voice and text bots with intents and slots in one service; Azure splits intent models (CLU, the successor to the retired LUIS) from bot building (Copilot Studio or Bot Service).

pairs.a: (no current Azure service; Azure AI Personalizer retired 2026-08-25)
pairs.difference: Personalize trains recommendation and segmentation models from interaction data; Microsoft retired Personalizer and points to the open-source learning-loop project.
All are AI coding assistants with agent modes in the IDE and CLI; Kiro is a spec-driven agentic IDE and Q Developer adds AWS console and transformation features (check current status of both).
